Old Ground

Old Ground

Wisconsin, Minnesota and Michigan in one map, with every detecting spot numbered 1 to 5 by how likely its old ground survives (1 is best; see the Undisturbed tab), plus lode targets, gold streams and traps, panning spots, gold reports, glacial gravel, pits, float copper, Lake Superior beaches, historic copper mines, ancient copper pits, historic sites, treasure stories, detecting sites, the rules for every kind of public land, a magnetic map, a three-state gold model, known metal deposits, Minnesota gold drilling, and glacial transport lines that trace glacial gold back to its source belt. Start with the picks, switch layers or pick a state, and tap any marker, gold stream or belt for its story. Pins were rechecked against Google Maps and USGS place and mine records, 633 spots carry a 0.6 m aerial photo and 241 a 1 m LiDAR view; each spot says how exact its pin is.

Distances are from Eau Claire.

Burial mounds, graves and cemeteries are never on this map, and ancient copper pits appear only at area level for the big picture; all are protected by Wisconsin, Minnesota, Michigan and federal law. Minnesota state parks ban detectors, Wisconsin DNR land allows them only to find a specific lost item with a permit, Michigan parks allow them only in designated areas, and national parks, wilderness and tribal land are look-only without permission. Many pins are approximate; each spot says how exact its pin is.

Field skills

Gold in Wisconsin and Minnesota is mostly flour gold riding with black sand. These notes come from the Field Book and the atlases, condensed for the creek bank.

Quick card

  • Gold follows greenstone. Lode gold sits in old volcanic belts: Wisconsin's Ladysmith–Rhinelander belt, Minnesota's Vermilion, Wawa and Rainy Lake belts, Michigan's Ishpeming–Michigamme belt.
  • Glaciers spread it. Ice scraped those belts and dropped fine gold in till, outwash and river gravel far away. To find a source, trace up-ice, not only upstream.
  • Eau Claire's gold came from the north-northeast, out of the Rusk County volcanic belt that held the Flambeau mine at Ladysmith (334,000 oz of gold, 1993–1997).
  • Expect flour gold. A nugget is a rare event and a newspaper story.
  • The Driftless Area never saw ice. Treat gold reports from southwest Wisconsin with extra suspicion.
  • Rules differ by land and by state. Read the Rules tab before you dig. National parks are look-only everywhere.
  • Never disturb graves, mounds or ancient copper pits.

Where gold settles

Gold is about 19 times heavier than water, so it drops wherever water slows. Find the slowdown, then dig to the bottom of the gravel. Best first:

  1. Cracked bedrock in fast water, especially just below falls and dams.
  2. The head (upstream end) of the first gravel bar below a steep stretch.
  3. Inside bends, where the current slows.
  4. Behind big boulders and bedrock ribs.
  5. Moss and grass roots at the high-water line, which catch flour gold.
  6. Where a gold-scored stream meets a bigger one.

Glacial gravel

Outwash plains, old channels, terraces, eskers and moraines hold reworked glacial gold. Gravel pits on them are the easiest place to pan, with the owner's permission. Pits on or just down-ice of a volcanic belt carry more local material.

Cheap tricks that work

  • Moss mining: strip moss off rocks at the high-water line, wash it in a tub, pan the residue.
  • Fresh flood bars: spring high water re-sorts gravel, so the first visit after a flood is best.
  • Scour spots: bridge piers, culvert outlets and gravel-road ditches concentrate heavies.
  • Beaver dams: pan just below old dams.
  • Reservoir drawdowns: Holcombe Flowage drops up to 10 ft in late winter and exposes shoreline gravel.
  • Gravel-plant fines: with permission, pan the fine sand from the screen deck or settling pond. It samples thousands of tons at once.

Best boulder country near Eau Claire

The Chippewa Moraine south of New Auburn, the Perkinstown moraine from Otter Lake to Cornell, and the till plains around Seevers' 1948 gold creek near New Auburn. Dig under and between boulder lags; heavies stay with the boulders.

Reading the gravel

You seeWhat it tells you
Black sand (magnetite)A working trap. Gold travels with it, but black sand alone is not proof. At Silver Bay, MN the black beach is taconite waste.
Pink-red garnet grainsAnother heavy-mineral sign. Garnet came with the gold at Plum Creek.
Blue-gray or tan clay under gravelFalse bedrock. Pan the inch of gravel resting on it.
Orange and rust bandsOld water tables and weathered pyrite. Rusty quartz pebbles are worth a crush test.
White vein quartz with rust or dark specksThe kind of rock that carries lode gold.
Tight cobble pavementFast water sorted it; fines are trapped underneath.
Red basalt and agatesThe gravel came from the Lake Superior copper country.
Rusty quartz with boxy holes, pyrite-bearing greenstoneIndicator float. A train of such boulders points up-ice (north to northeast here).

Sampling routine

  1. Test-pan 2 or 3 pans per spot before setting up a sluice. No color and no black sand: move on.
  2. For flour gold, run a fine-riffle or matting sluice at a low angle with slow water. Steep, fast boxes lose it.
  3. Save every cleanup. Classify to minus 30 mesh and pull magnetite with a magnet in a bag.
  4. Finish concentrates at home on a blue bowl or wheel.
  5. Log GPS, pan count and color count for every sample. After a few trips the log tells you which reach to work.
What a flake is worth. Gold was about $4,166 an ounce on Oct 16, 2026, so one gram is about $134. Most Wisconsin creeks carry fine gold; flakes are rare.

Panning step by step

  1. Fill the pan with gravel from a trap: inside bends, the downstream side of boulders, bedrock cracks.
  2. Sink it under water, break up any clay with your fingers, and rinse and toss out the big rocks.
  3. Shake hard side to side under water so the heavy stuff drops to the bottom.
  4. Tilt the pan away and wash off the top layer with a circular "racetrack" swirl, thumb on the lip. Shake and wash again until only black sand is left.
  5. Strip the magnetite with a magnet wrapped in paper (pull the magnet out and the sand drops off).
  6. Tip the gold onto a creased piece of paper and slide it into a vial, or suck it up with a snuffer bottle.

Burn the factory oil off a new steel pan over a fire before you use it; gold slides on oil. Look over the black sand for red garnet, honey-colored zircon and the odd ruby-red grain. Never use mercury, and sell raw gold only to a licensed buyer.

What the gold tells you

  • Flour gold and rounded grains come from placers and have travelled. Keep working the gravel.
  • Leaf and wire gold breaks off veins and doesn't travel far, so the source is close. Look upstream and uphill.
  • Pale gold carries more silver.
  • Old prospectors looked for old benches above today's river, sinkholes, odd-colored ground and ground someone had worked before, and took samples to a school of mines to compare.

From Dwyer, Summer Gold.

Fool's gold check

TestGoldPyriteMica
Pin pokeDents and bendsShattersFlakes apart
Swirl in the panStays put on the bottomMoves with sandFloats and flashes
Turn it in the lightButter-yellow from every angleBrassy, sharp facesFlashes, then goes dark

Store-bought play or construction sand is washed quartz from industrial pits; any gold in it is a curiosity. Crushed quarry rock (driveway rock, road base, Dresser trap rock) never sat in a stream and holds no placer gold.

Old-timers' gold tests

  • Turn it in the light. Gold keeps its color from every angle and in shade.
  • Hammer it. Gold flattens; pyrite and chalcopyrite shatter into dark powder.
  • Feel the weight. Gold is 19.3 times as heavy as water, about seven times a rock its size. At hardness 2.5 to 3, a knife cuts it.
  • Read the rock. Lode gold rides in rusty, honeycombed quartz, often where quartz meets granite, slate or quartzite. Limestone country rarely holds any, except glacial gold carried in.

From Coffman (1957) and Dwyer. The ID guide has full gold, pyrite and black sand entries.

Reading old ground: what the 1800s books teach

From a page-by-page read (Oct. 2026) of Sawyer, History of the Northern Peninsula of Michigan (1911), Upham, Minnesota Geographic Names (1920) and the Wisconsin Historical Collections vol. II (1856).

Finding old copper and iron ground

  • Ancient pits run in lines. Every big Keweenaw and Ontonagon mine (Minesota, Winona, Cliff, Central) was found by following Indian pits along the outcrop. Look for a continuous shallow trench or a row of rounded, moss-filled hollows along a trap ridge, filled flush with washed clay and leaf mould, with low spoil heaps beside them that break the natural slope. Trees on the spoil are as big as the forest around them. Grooved stone mauls (beach cobbles with a pecked groove for a withe handle) lie in the fill. Knapp found the Minesota pits in 1847 this way, and a six-ton copper mass still on its log skids under a 400-ring hemlock.
  • A compass that goes crazy. Burt's survey crew found the Negaunee iron in 1844 because the needle swung wildly and reversed. A cheap magnetic compass (or a phone magnetometer app) that misbehaves while you walk a line means magnetic iron formation within a few hundred yards.
  • Green water. Alexander Henry (1771) followed a green-stained seep to copper. Malachite crusts on weathered rock and a seep that plates a bare nail copper-colored mean copper near the surface. Native copper in amygdaloid hugs the hanging wall and runs down the bed in diagonal "copper courses".
  • Drift-covered ranges. Around Iron River and Stambaugh the ore lies under thick till with no outcrops; the old-timers found it with test pits clustered along the river valleys and draws. Expect rows of old prospect pits in the draws.
  • Shore landings and sled roads. The 1845 to 1855 mines were tied to the lake by winter sled roads and shore landings that predate every road on the later maps. Find them on the 1840s to 1850s surveys and work the landing.

Lead-region signs (1827 prospectors)

  • Old Indian diggings show as small aspen clumps on up-turned clay.
  • "Gravel mineral": water-worn, carbonized lumps of galena, sometimes pounds in weight, point to ore on the adjacent highland.
  • Masonic weed (leadplant, Amorpha canescens) grows rank over deep clay and rock crevices.
  • Sucker holes: clusters of shallow prospect pits on a hillside; cabins and dumps crowd where a vein was struck. Smelter ash beds were also the stores where miners traded, so coins turn up around furnaces.

Other ground to read

  • Glacial beach ridges. Glacial Lake Aitkin's ridge of sand and gravel, 3 to 5 feet high, is the dry ground the old roads and camps followed. Glacial Lake Duluth's highest beach stands 470 feet above Superior at Duluth and 510 feet on Mount Josephine: a flat gravel terrace on the hillside anywhere on the North Shore.
  • Rice and Sugar Bush lakes. Lakes named Rice, Manomin or Sugar Bush were seasonal Indian camps; lodges stood on the shore above the rice beds.
  • Painted Rocks. A lone glacial boulder on open prairie with a Painted Rock name was a Dakota offering stone. Generations of passers-by left small things around it.
  • First-fall mills. Every early mill in western Wisconsin (1818 to 1831) sat at the first fall of a pine river, and nearly every dam was swept out within a year or two, leaving irons and crew camps.
  • Charcoal kilns show as rings of brick or stone, or round earthen mounds, in rows near a creek or rail spur within a few miles of a blast furnace; the soil stays black for decades.
  • Splash dams sit where a drivable creek narrows above a rapids: cribbing timbers, cut banks, the camp on the high ground, and lost gear at the jam points below.
  • Placer gold in the drift. The Minnesota survey found traces of placer gold in the glacial drift on branches of the Zumbro and Root rivers; settlers washed it at Sacramento in 1855. Test inside bends and bedrock riffles below Mantorville.
  • Prairie du Chien claim plats. The French farm lots run in strips from the river to the bluffs; the 1828 government survey of private claims maps each one. Pull those plats before working any old house site on the prairie.

Reading a county plat book

  • The key. In the 1893 Clark County book (and most plat books of the time): a square with an X is a schoolhouse, an empty square a town hall, a triangle a church, a star a mill, a little headstone a cemetery, and hatching means land cut into village lots. A black dot or small square on a farm is a house or barn.
  • Owners' names. Each parcel carries its owner and acres. A shortened name is spelled out elsewhere in the same township. The name tells you whose farm a school or cheese factory sat on, which is what the old county histories and obituaries use.
  • Find the corner schools. Country schools sat on a corner of a farm at a road crossing, usually on a quarter acre. When the plat puts a schoolhouse square on a corner where nothing stands today, that corner is a strong spot: the yard, the privy pit and the path to the road.
  • Dams and mills on the river. A star or a dam line across a river where today's map shows only water or woods marks a logging dam or sawmill. The crew camp, store and dump were on the high bank beside it.
  • Dashed lines are roads; many were later moved or closed. An old road that ran to a vanished school, mill or store is the path the people walked.
  • Plat books map type. Turn it on to lay the books over today's map (see-through slider). The pins marked "1893 plat" or "1913 plat" are read from them. Accuracy is about 100 to 150 m, so walk the ground around the pin.

Caves, old mines and bad air

  • Never enter old mine workings. Rotten timber, hidden shafts, water and bad air kill experienced people.
  • Firedamp (methane) gathers up high, at head height and above. Chokedamp (carbon dioxide) pools on the floor and in low spots. You can't see either one.
  • In caves, carry a gas meter, tell someone where you are, and turn back at any headache, dizziness or shortness of breath.
  • Show and park caves (Cherney Maribel, Cave of the Mounds): carry three lights, stay out of gated caves without a guide, never touch or break formations, and clean boots and gear between caves (white-nose syndrome kills Wisconsin bats). Caves in parks are look only: no digging, no detecting, no collecting.

When to go

Late August through September, at low water. Example: the Eau Claire River at Kelly runs about 113–127 cfs in August–September against a 612 cfs peak in April. Check the USGS gauge before you drive, and stay out of channels below dams with scheduled releases (Jim Falls has whitewater releases through the old channel).

Gear

Day pack

  • Two pans (a 14-inch for classifying, a 10-inch for finishing) and a 1/4-inch classifier screen.
  • Crevice tool or old screwdriver, a stiff brush, and a snuffer bottle.
  • A short shovel, a 5-gallon bucket, and a small tub for moss mining.
  • A strong magnet in a zip bag for stripping black sand.
  • Vials for color, a hand lens, and a notebook or phone for the sample log.
  • Waders or neoprene boots, and this guide saved for offline use.

Beyond the pan

ToolFindsLimits
VLF-EMSteep conductors like sulfide lenses and faults; cheap, quick linesShallow, fooled by fences, pipes and power lines
Ground magnetometerMagnetic rock and pyrrhotite; pairs with USGS magnetic gridsCrandon-type ore can be non-magnetic
Soil-gas samplingGases from buried sulfides through tillNeeds a lab; varies with weather
Silt or basal-till assayTellurium, arsenic, bismuth, antimony pathfindersLab cost

Metal detecting

  • Go where crowds waited. Fairgrounds midways, drive-in lots, swimming beaches, ferry landings, ballparks and interurban stops. The Detecting chips on the map hold these.
  • Find the exact old footprint. Compare 1930s–1990s aerial photos (WHAIFinder for Wisconsin, MHAPO for Minnesota) and old USGS topos with today's map. Unbuilt corners of old grounds are the prime ground.
  • Beaches: work the towel line and the drop-off in late summer and after storms. Check each beach's own rules; Minnesota state parks ban detectors, and Michigan parks allow them only in designated areas.
  • Ghost towns and CCC camps: most sit on private or county forest land. Get written permission, and leave anything on state land that is 50 or more years old.
  • Fill every hole, pack out trash, and show the owner anything good you find.
  • Swing low and level, about 2 inches off the ground. Ground wet from rain or morning dew lets the signal reach deeper.
  • Dig every signal. Old silver comes up looking like a black iron button, copper a sickly green, and gold dust from a rotted poke a lumpy black "bug's nest".

Where homesteaders hid money

Fence posts near the house, foundation corners, hollow tree crotches, inside walls, and above door headers, especially the front door and the bedroom door. Search only with the owner's written okay.

Small finds that date a site

  • Hand-forged square nails mean an early building.
  • Buttons, brass and military ones especially, mark camps and old homes.
  • Bottles and old dumps show where people lived and roughly when.
  • Coins and tokens date the ground best. The ID guide's coin pages give dates and values.

From Dwyer and Coffman.

Drive mode

For a phone on a dash mount. Open it from the + button or More > Drive mode. The map tilts and turns so the road ahead points up, the screen stays on, and the dark panel shows the ranked spots ahead of you (Best, Good and Some old ground, from the layers you have on) with distance, which side of the road, and the main reason. Navigate hands the spot to Google Maps or Apple Maps for turn-by-turn directions.

  • Set it up before you roll. Pick your layers, Google or Apple Maps, and voice on or off while parked. Don't tap through cards while driving: let a passenger do it, or pull over. Voice reads out a spot once when it is within 3 miles ahead.
  • Mount the phone low where it doesn't block the road, and keep it plugged in. GPS and a lit screen drain a battery fast. After 10 minutes parked, the screen is allowed to sleep; tap it to keep driving.
  • A spot ahead is not permission. Most pins sit on private land or public land with rules. Read the card's access notes and ask before you detect.
  • No CarPlay. Apple only lets approved native apps onto the car screen, so Old Ground can't show there. Navigate opens Google Maps or Apple Maps, which do show on CarPlay, with the spot as the destination.
  • Drag the map to look around; Re-center picks you back up. With no signal, the cards and GPS still work, and the map shows the areas you saved offline.

Chasing legends

Every spot carries a confidence tag. Read it before you plan a trip:

Documented recordA survey, assay, state file or museum record backs it.
Newspaper storyPrinted at the time, often exaggerated, sometimes the only record.
LegendRetold for generations. The setting is real; the treasure may not be.
Forum rumorUnverified. Use it as a reason to search old papers, not to dig.
Computer model ideaAn untested area the gold model scored high.

Start with county histories and old newspapers to pin the place, then check land ownership on the county parcel map before you set foot there. Robbery loot and found caches can still have legal owners.

Clubs and people

  • Wausau Prospectors (GPAA chapter): first Saturday of each month at 11 AM. Phone (715) 340-2831, or their Facebook page.
  • Twin Cities Prospectors (GPAA): (612) 245-6569.
  • GPAA chapters also meet in Tomah and Greenbush.
  • Well drillers, gravel-pit operators and county foresters see bedrock, sulfides and rusty water first. Bring a printed map.

Glossary

Black sandHeavy dark minerals (mostly magnetite) that settle with gold
CrevicingScraping and brushing out bedrock cracks for gold
Driftless AreaSW Wisconsin and nearby, never covered by the last ice
EskerA winding gravel ridge left by a river under the ice
False bedrockA clay or hardpan layer that stops gold like bedrock does
FloatLoose rock or metal moved away from its source
Flour goldGold so fine it looks like dust; the usual Midwest find
GossanRusty, weathered cap over a sulfide body
GreenstoneOld altered volcanic rock, the host of most lode gold
LodeGold still in bedrock (veins, shear zones)
MoraineA ridge of till at a glacier's edge
OutwashSand and gravel washed out from melting ice; good panning ground
PlacerGold freed from rock and concentrated by water
Poor rockMine waste piles where copper country collectors pick
TillUnsorted glacial debris, from clay to boulders
Tunnel channelA valley cut by water flowing under the ice
Up-iceThe direction the glacier came from; where to look for the source

Offline use

Everything here, including the map, is built into this one page. Nothing loads from the internet except the fonts, which fall back to your phone's own. You are in the home-screen app: the whole atlas, old maps included, is saved on this phone, and it updates itself when you have signal. Google Maps and source links still need a connection. The old-map slider pictures (1936, 1972 and today) load from the online atlas, so open the slider once with a signal; the offline copy does not have them. Finds, worked marks and river levels save to your atlas when you are online and to your phone when you are not.

Finds log

Every visit you log from a spot's details. Logging empty trips matters too: it tells the weekly update which spots don't pay.

Rules by state

A summary of the rules that decide where you can pan, detect and collect. Agencies change rules; call the land manager before a first visit.

WisconsinMinnesotaMichiganLakesFederal and tribalWho owns a findOld land lawEtiquette

Wisconsin

  • Hand tools only, no permit, if you don't sell what you find and move under 2 cubic yards per waterway per year. Any motor (pump, dredge, highbanker) needs a permit.
  • Bank owners own to mid-stream. Get permission to cross or work the bank.
  • No collecting at all in state parks, state trails, recreation areas, Wild Rivers (Pine, Popple and Brule), State Natural Areas, or state-owned lakebeds, including the Lake Superior bed.
  • Other DNR land needs a collector's permit (5 lb a day, 50 lb a year).
  • Metal detectors on DNR land are allowed only to find a specific lost item, with a permit.
  • Objects 50 or more years old found on state land stay where they are.
  • Eau Claire County parks and forest ban removing rocks without written permission. Big Falls and Lowes Creek fall under this.
  • Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest: ask the ranger district first.

Minnesota

  • Hand panning needs no permit in state-owned stream, river and lake beds, including the North Shore lakebed.
  • No panning or collecting in state parks, and metal detectors are banned in all state parks.
  • Trout streams: call DNR fisheries before you disturb the bed.
  • Boundary Waters (BWCA) is closed to collecting.
  • 2026 mining changes: Executive Order 26-10 (Aug 18, 2026) bans new nonferrous mining permits in the Rainy River Headwaters, and the DNR cancelled one Twin Metals lease near Babbitt on Sept 12. They don’t change hobby panning rules.

Michigan

  • Panning on state land is allowed where the state owns the minerals, but not on trout streams or designated natural rivers.
  • Great Lakes shores and bottomlands are closed to panning.
  • Rock collecting on state and public trust land is capped at 25 lb a year.
  • State parks allow detecting only in designated areas. F.J. McLain bans it.
  • Keweenaw mine rock piles are private. The Cliff piles and Mineral Days are the open exceptions.
  • Ottawa National Forest rules apply on forest land.

Turn on the Lakes layer on the map for a pin on each, with sources.

Lake and lakebed rules, rechecked Oct. 26, 2026
  • Minnesota: hand panning with non-mechanical tools needs no state permit in state-owned lake, stream and river beds. It is not allowed where mineral collecting is banned, such as state parks, and a designated trout stream needs a call to the Area Fisheries Manager first. Sluices and dredges are commercial: they need the mineral owner's permission and state permits. (MN DNR)
  • Wisconsin: mineral collection is not allowed on lakebeds the state owns, or in state parks, trails, recreation areas, wild and scenic rivers and natural areas. On other DNR land you may need a collector's permit, generally 5 lb a day and 50 lb a year. Manual dredging under 2 cubic yards per waterway per year needs no water permit, and powered dredges need a permit. Metal detectors on DNR land are only for finding a specific lost item, with a permit, May 1 to Oct. 15. (WI DNR panning, detectors)
  • Michigan: recreational panning only on state land where the state owns both surface and minerals. Great Lakes shores and bottomlands, designated trout streams, natural rivers and natural areas are closed. Power sluicing is banned and a sluice needs an EGLE permit. (MI DNR)
  • National parks and lakeshores: collecting rocks, driftwood and artifacts is not allowed at the Apostle Islands, and the same federal park rules apply at Voyageurs and Isle Royale. Call the park before bringing a detector. (NPS)

Rules change. Call the managing office before a first trip.

Federal and tribal land

  • National parks and lakeshores are look-only (36 CFR 2.1): Isle Royale, Voyageurs, Apostle Islands, Pictured Rocks and the St. Croix riverway.
  • Wilderness areas and underwater shipwreck preserves: no collecting.
  • ARPA protects archaeological material on federal land. Never dig artifacts there.
  • Tribal lands need the tribe's permission for any entry beyond public roads.
  • Never dig burial mounds, graves, cemeteries or ancient copper pits. State and federal law protect them everywhere.
Mineral rights can sit apart from the surface. Wisconsin's dormant mineral law (Wis. Stat. 706.057) and released exploration data (107.15) are covered in the Field Book research chapter.

Who owns what you find

  • The US has no treasure-trove law. Courts sort finds into lost (dropped by accident), mislaid (put somewhere on purpose and forgotten) and abandoned (thrown away or given up). Which one a find is decides who keeps it, and mislaid property usually goes to the landowner.
  • Trespassers lose the find. Anything found while trespassing goes to the landowner.
  • Get it in writing. A permission note names you and the owner, says what you will search for and where, and sets the split before you dig. Owners usually ask 10 to 25%.
  • Minerals belong to the landowner unless the mineral rights were sold off separately. The county register of deeds shows it.
  • Mining claims don't apply here. Placer claims under the 1872 Mining Law (20 acres per person, 160 acres for a group of 8) exist only on federal public-domain land, nearly all of it in the West. In the Midwest, permission is what counts.
  • Reading a legal description. Land is surveyed in townships 6 miles square, each split into 36 numbered sections of 1 square mile. "NE¼ Sec. 12, T27N, R9W" points to one quarter-section, which is how old reports and plat maps place a site.

From Coffman, 1001 Lost, Buried or Sunken Treasures (1957), and Dwyer, Summer Gold. Not legal advice.

Old land law, and why it matters for a site today

  • Burials. Wisconsin (s. 157.70), Minnesota (307.08) and Michigan law protect all human burials, marked or not, on any land. Northern Indian graves were often shallow under a bark "spirit house" with a carved post; copper, trade silver or beads with bone means a burial. Stop, backfill, and report to the state archaeologist.
  • 1826 Fond du Lac treaty. First gave the United States the right "to search and carry away any metals or minerals" from Chippewa land without changing title; the 1842 treaty (ratified 1843) ceded the rest of the U.P. and Isle Royale and opened the surveys.
  • Copper-country titles. 1843 to 1847 mineral ground was held under federal permits and leases "without authority of law", in huge overlapping locations held by leaving a few men on the ground over winter. From 1847 it was sold outright by patent, which is why nearly all Keweenaw and Ontonagon mineral land is private today, and why 1840s "claim" names on old maps don't match later patents. Check the GLO patent record before trusting a mine name's location.
  • Tract books, not deeds. In the 1860s to 70s U.P., even sections along the ranges were withdrawn for canal and railroad grants; private entries used agricultural scrip and cash at $1.25 an acre, and "buy a forty and cut a section" was common. The GLO tract books show who first held an old camp or pit.
  • Lead lands before 1832 were a federal mineral reserve: a miner needed a permit, paid rent in mineral to a licensed smelter, and could not farm. 1827 to 1832 sites are dug-out hovels and furnace ash beds, not farmsteads.
  • Claim unions of 1836. Before the land sales, settlers at Pike River (Kenosha) and Milwaukee ran their own claim law: one quarter section each, marked by a house frame or a half acre ploughed, recorded with the union clerk for $2, disputes settled by elected arbitrators "peaceably if can be, and forcibly if must be". Their claim maps are a settlement-site source.
  • Land-office dates. Menominee valley land was not open to purchase until the mid-1850s (surveys from 1839), pine at $1.25 an acre, first come first served: the big mills all date from 1856-57. The Menominee cessions ran 1831-32, 1836, 1848 and 1854, so original survey plats south of the Menominee-Escanaba line start in the late 1830s.

From Sawyer (1911), Upham (1920) and the Wisconsin Historical Collections vol. II (1856). Not legal advice.

Etiquette

  • Ask first, in person if you can, and say exactly what you'll do.
  • Fill holes, put rocks back, and leave banks as you found them.
  • Stay out of the water during dam releases and high flows.
  • Share what you find with the landowner. It is how you get invited back.

·

Gold in Wisconsin, Minnesota and Michigan is real but small: mostly flour-size grains that glaciers and rivers carried from old volcanic belts, plus a handful of lode districts up north. This book gathers everything from the gold atlases, maps and research notes into one field reference: the geology, the rules, the places, the stories and the tools. Carry it, read a chapter before a trip, and use the index at the back to look up any place or term.

Index A to Z

Chapter 1: Quick-reference card
  1. Gold follows greenstone. Nearly all lode gold in WI, MN and MI sits in ancient volcanic "greenstone" belts: Wisconsin's Ladysmith–Rhinelander belt, Minnesota's Vermilion, Wawa and Rainy Lake belts, and Michigan's Ishpeming–Michigamme belt.
  2. Glaciers spread it. Ice scraped those belts and dropped fine gold in till, outwash and river gravel hundreds of km away. To find the source, trace up-ice, not just upstream.
  3. Eau Claire's gold came from the north-northeast. Chippewa Valley gold traces back into the Rusk County volcanic belt, the one that held the Flambeau mine at Ladysmith.
  4. Flambeau proved it. The Flambeau open pit (1993–1997) produced 181,000 tons of copper, 334,000 oz of gold and 3.3 million oz of silver.
  5. Expect flour gold. Pans here mostly show tiny flakes with black sand. A nugget is a rare event and a newspaper story.
  6. Pan the traps. Bedrock cracks below falls and dams, the head of gravel bars, inside bends, and where steep water flattens. Go at low water, August–September.
  7. The Driftless Area never saw ice. SW Wisconsin gold reports can't be glacial; treat them with extra suspicion.
  8. Wisconsin DNR land is strict. No mineral collecting on state parks, trails, recreation areas, wild rivers, natural areas or state-owned lakebeds (including the Lake Superior bed). Metal detectors only to find a specific lost item, with a permit.
  9. Minnesota allows hand panning in state-owned stream, river and lake beds, but not in state parks. Detectors are banned in Minnesota state parks.
  10. Michigan closes Great Lakes shores and bottomlands to panning. There's a 25 lb a year rock limit on state and public trust land. State parks allow detecting only in designated areas.
  11. National parks are look-only. 36 CFR 2.1 bars collecting and detecting in every NPS unit (Isle Royale, Voyageurs, Apostle Islands, Pictured Rocks).
  12. Never disturb graves, mounds or ancient copper pits. They are protected by state and federal law.
  13. Copper country is next door. The Keweenaw holds float copper, legal-to-pick rock piles, and ancient copper pits; Isle Royale has more than 1,000 prehistoric pits, about 4,500 years old.
  14. Most promising rock is buried. In much of Minnesota, gold-favorable bedrock lies under 250–970 ft of glacial sediment. Only drilling reaches it.
  15. Follow the pros. Newmont, AngloGold Ashanti, Vermillion Gold and others drilled northern Minnesota; their clusters are the best public hint of where gold might be.
Chapter 2: How gold got here

Gold formed in old volcanic belts, then glaciers ground it up and spread it south. Knowing both steps tells you where to look.

The bedrock belts (the source)

  • Archean greenstone, about 2.7 billion years old: Minnesota's Vermilion, Wawa and Rainy Lake belts, plus belts in Michigan's Upper Peninsula and Ontario (Rainy Lake–Seine River, Wabigoon, Shebandowan, Beardmore–Geraldton, Hemlo, Wawa–Michipicoten).
  • Paleoproterozoic volcanic belts, about 1.8–1.9 billion years old: Wisconsin's belt from Ladysmith through Rhinelander to Pembine and Michigan's Back Forty area. These host the Flambeau, Bend, Reef, Lynne, Crandon and Back Forty deposits.
  • Keweenawan rift rocks, about 1.1 billion years old: basalt and conglomerate around Lake Superior. They hold native copper and silver, not much gold.
  • Paleozoic sandstone and limestone in southern WI and MN and most of lower Michigan carry essentially no gold of their own.

The glaciers (the delivery truck)

Each ice lobe moved in its own direction, so the source of glacial gold lies up-ice from where you find it. The atlas's glacial transport lines draw this for 75 spots.

Ice lobeWhere it coveredIce came fromLikely source belt for its gold
Chippewa lobeChippewa Valley, Eau Claire to CornellNorth-northeastRusk and Sawyer County volcanic belt (Flambeau)
Superior lobeNW Wisconsin, east-central Minnesota, St. CroixNortheast, down the Lake Superior basinRusk/Sawyer belts, and far up-ice Ontario's Beardmore–Geraldton belt
Rainy lobeNE MinnesotaNorth-northeastVermilion and Rainy Lake belts, Ontario's Rainy Lake–Seine River belt
Des Moines and Wadena lobesWestern and southern MinnesotaNorth-northwestBuried western Minnesota greenstone
Wisconsin Valley and Langlade lobesNorth-central WisconsinNorth to northeastRhinelander and Forest County volcanic belts
Green Bay and Lake Michigan lobesEastern WisconsinNorth-northeast to northPembine–Athelstane (Marinette County) belt
Lake Michigan and Saginaw lobesLower MichiganNorthOntario's Wawa–Michipicoten belt, 300–650 km away

Directions are generalized per lobe; older glaciations and rivers also moved gold.

The Driftless Area of SW Wisconsin and SE Minnesota escaped the last ice. Gold there can't be glacial, so most "gold" reports there deserve a hard second look (pyrite and mica fool people).

Chapter 3: The red drift: Lake Superior material near home

The Superior lobe ground up the copper- and gold-bearing rock around western Lake Superior and spread it south as red till, sand and gravel. Its older advance (the River Falls phase) reached Hudson, Menomonie and Foster, about 20 miles from Eau Claire. Most of the gold reports west of Eau Claire sit on this red drift.

How to recognize it

  • Red or brick-colored till and sand, from Lake Superior sandstone and basalt.
  • Red Keweenawan basalt, gabbro and rhyolite pebbles, and Lake Superior agates. The older River Falls outwash in western Chippewa County is up to about 35 m thick and carries big agates.
  • Agates on the Chippewa River bars below Durand prove Superior gravel reached them.

The source rock up north

SourceCountyWhat the record says
Chippewa mine, Douglas copper rangeDouglasCrane (1908): gold in diabase ledges, $2 to $11 a ton
Federal Copper propertyDouglas1902 assay: native gold flakes in diabase at $9 a ton
Davis Hill conglomerateBayfieldGold with silver and copper in conglomerate north of Namekagon Lake
Holmes and Baraba prospects, Penokee RangeAshland1902: shafts 150 and 188 ft, a 40-ft gossan, assays to $3 gold and 9 oz silver a ton; Baraba 2.8% copper with gold traces
Chicago Mine and Northern Belle, Penokee GapAshlandGold, copper and silver worked briefly in 1879–1881; a placer attempt on Brunschweiler Creek in the 1880s

The Lake Duluth flood channel

When glacial Lake Duluth filled the western Superior basin, it drained southwest through the Brule valley into the St. Croix. Everything that flood carried passed Upper St. Croix Lake at Solon Springs first, where the old Brule–St. Croix portage crosses the divide. Flood gravel straight out of the Superior basin lines the spillway, and the St. Croix Dalles at the bottom of the channel is the best-documented placer in the region (gold flakes and nuggets in basalt cracks).

Best red-drift spots to pan

  • St. Croix Dalles basalt crevices, and the glacial drift north of St. Croix Falls (WGNHS reports flakes in both).
  • Rock Elm and Plum creeks, Pierce County: worked 1887–1890, diamonds recovered, gold confirmed again in 1985.
  • Hawthorne, Poplar and Middle River placers below the Douglas copper range.
  • Amnicon Falls and Big Manitou Falls (Black River, Pattison): falls over cracked basalt on the Douglas fault, natural crevice traps. Both are in state parks, so under Wisconsin rules they are look only.
  • Copper Falls and Brownstone Falls on the Bad River and Tyler Forks, just below the Penokee prospects (state park, look only).
  • Black-sand streaks on Port Wing, Herbster and Wisconsin Point beaches after storms (an untested idea; the Lake Superior bed is closed to collecting in Wisconsin).
  • Gravel pits in red drift, with the operator's permission.

Glacial landmarks of the Superior lobe

  • Foster, Eau Claire County: the southern edge of the older Superior ice, the closest red drift to Eau Claire.
  • The St. Croix moraine and Spooner Hills tunnel channels, where the late ice stood.
  • The Emerald phase limit in St. Croix County, the farthest late Superior ice.
  • Glacial Lake Grantsburg basin, where deltas dropped coarse heavy sand first.
  • Cumberland, Barron County: farmers reported gold nuggets in 1905 (poorly documented); the old Barron Quartzite crops out nearby.
Chapter 4: Where to look and how

Gold is about 19 times heavier than water, so it drops wherever water slows down. Find the slowdown, then dig to the bottom of the gravel.

Placer traps, best first

  1. Cracked bedrock in fast water, especially just below falls and dams (the river scours down to rock and packs heavy sand into the cracks).
  2. The head (upstream end) of the first gravel bar below a steep stretch.
  3. Inside bends, where the current slows.
  4. Behind big boulders and bedrock ribs.
  5. Moss and grass roots at the high-water line (they catch flour gold).
  6. Where a gold-scored stream meets a bigger one.

Glacial gravel

  • Outwash plains, old channels, terraces, eskers and moraines hold reworked glacial gold. Gravel pits on them are the easiest place to pan, with the owner's permission.
  • Pits sitting on or just down-ice of a volcanic belt carry more local material than pits on far-traveled drift.

Field habits

  • Go at low water, August to September.
  • Black sand (magnetite) is your friend: gold travels with it. Keep your concentrates and work them at home.
  • Rusty quartz, sulfide-bearing (pyrite) float boulders and sheared rock are signs of a lode source up-ice or upstream.
  • Fool's gold (pyrite) is brassy and shatters; mica flakes float and flash. Real gold stays put, looks butter-yellow from every angle, and bends under a pin.

Bagged sand? People do pan bags of play or construction sand from stores like Menards. It's washed quartz from industrial pits, so treat any gold in it as a curiosity, not a source.

Reading the gravel and banks

  • Black sand (magnetite, ilmenite): black streaks on bar heads or a dark smear in the pan. More black sand means a better trap. Black sand alone is not proof of gold; at Silver Bay, Minnesota the black beach is taconite waste.
  • Red garnet sand: pink-red grains with the black sand, another heavy-mineral sign. Garnet came with the gold, diamonds, topaz and platinum at Plum Creek.
  • Clay layers (false bedrock): blue-gray or tan clay under gravel stops gold just like bedrock. Pan the inch of gravel resting on it.
  • Iron staining: orange and rust bands mark old water tables and weathered pyrite. Rusty quartz pebbles are worth a crush test.
  • White vein quartz, especially rusty or with dark specks: a piece of the kind of rock that carries lode gold.
  • Tight cobble pavements: fast water sorted them, and fines got trapped underneath.
  • Red basalt and agates: the gravel came from the Lake Superior copper country (Chapter 3).

Boulders

  • A lone erratic rarely holds gold; most are granite or gneiss.
  • Boulder lags: where water washed the sand away, heavies stayed with the boulders. Dig under and between them.
  • Indicator float: rusty vein quartz, pyrite-bearing greenstone or banded iron formation. Crush a sample and pan it. A train of such boulders points up-ice (north to northeast here).
  • Stream boulders: gold settles in the gravel at the downstream foot and in the crack where boulder meets bedrock.
  • Best boulder country near Eau Claire: the Chippewa Moraine south of New Auburn, the Perkinstown moraine from Otter Lake to Cornell, and the till plains around Seevers' 1948 gold creek near New Auburn.

More low-cost methods

  • Moss mining: strip moss off rocks at the high-water line, wash it in a tub, pan the residue. Moss catches flour gold during floods; the BC Geological Survey uses moss sampling too.
  • Fresh flood bars: spring high water re-sorts gravel; the first visit after a flood is best.
  • Scour spots: bridge piers, culvert outlets and gravel-road ditches concentrate heavies.
  • Beaver dams: ponds slow streams and drop heavy grains; pan just below old dams.
  • Plowed fields: plowing turns up float rock (the 110 lb Vienna meteorite was found picking rocks).
  • Gravel-plant fines: with permission, pan the fine sand from the screen deck or settling pond; it samples thousands of tons of glacial gravel at once. Bring a magnet for the magnetite.

Sampling routine

  1. Test-pan 2 to 3 pans per spot before setting up a sluice. No color and no black sand: move on.
  2. For flour gold, run a fine-riffle or matting sluice at a low angle and slow water; flour gold floats out of steep, fast boxes.
  3. Save every cleanup. Classify to minus 30 mesh, pull magnetite with a magnet in a bag, and finish on a blue bowl or wheel at home.
  4. Log GPS, pan count and color count for every sample. After a few trips the log tells you which reach to work.

Trucked-in material and store paydirt

  • Crushed quarry rock (driveway rock, road base, ballast, riprap, Dresser trap rock) never sat in a stream: no placer gold.
  • Washed decorative river rock from gold states is screened and washed, so the fines where flour gold rides are gone.
  • Local glacial sand and gravel is the real imported material: ice hauled it from Canada and the Superior basin, and meltwater sorted the heavies to the bottom of each layer.
  • Store-bought paydirt bags (Alaska, Klondike, Colorado) are a real way to pan gold at home; you pay roughly what the gold is worth, and some bags are salted, so buy from sellers who state the gold weight.

The numbers

  • One gram of gold was worth about $134 in October 2026 (gold about $4,166 an ounce on Oct 16, 2026).
  • The Wausau Prospectors' president put it simply: almost every Wisconsin creek has fine gold, but flakes are rare.
Chapter 5: Rules by land type

Private land with permission is always the safest bet; public land rules differ sharply by state. Check the current rule with the land manager before you dig, since these change.

LandPanning and collectingMetal detecting
Wisconsin DNR land (state parks, trails, recreation areas, wild rivers, natural areas)No mineral collectingOnly to find a specific lost item, with a property-manager permit
Wisconsin state-owned lakebeds, including the Lake Superior bedNo mineral collectingSame DNR rule
Minnesota state-owned stream, river and lake bedsHand panning allowedCheck locally
Minnesota state parksNo panning or collectingBanned
Michigan Great Lakes shores and bottomlandsClosed to panningCheck locally
Michigan state and public trust landRock collecting up to 25 lb a yearState parks: designated areas only (the Porcupine Mountains have some)
Ottawa National Forest (MI)Hand tools onlyGenerally allowed for casual use; ask the ranger district
National Park Service units (Isle Royale, Voyageurs, Apostle Islands, Pictured Rocks)Banned (36 CFR 2.1)Banned
Boundary Waters and other wildernessLook onlyLook only
Tribal reservationsOnly with tribal permissionOnly with tribal permission
Burial mounds, graves, cemeteries, ancient copper pitsNeverNever

Rules of thumb

  • Hand tools only: pan, shovel, classifier. No motorized dredges or sluice pumps without permits.
  • Fill your holes and stay out of banks, which erodes them.
  • Gravel pits, mine rock piles and farm fields are private: get permission every time.
  • Shipwreck preserves and anything historic on public land is off limits to take.

Wisconsin panning in detail

  • No DNR permit is needed for recreational panning with hand tools (pan, shovel, screen, small hand sluice, metal detector) if the gold is not for sale and you move less than 2 cubic yards of streambed per waterway per year.
  • Anything with a motor (dredge, pump, highbanker, powered excavation) needs a prospecting permit.
  • Riverbank owners own to the middle of the stream, including the streambed and the gold in it. Ask first.
  • Collecting is banned in state parks, state trails, state recreation areas, State Wild Rivers (including the Pine and Popple in Florence County), State Natural Areas and state-owned lakebeds. Some other DNR land allows rock collecting with a property manager's permit (5 lb a day, 50 lb a year).
  • Eau Claire County parks and forest prohibit disturbing or removing rocks and geological features (Big Falls and Lowes Creek fall under this). Get written permission.
  • National forest land: ask the ranger district.
  • Objects 50 or more years old found on state land must stay where they are found.
  • Below hydro dams, flows can jump without warning. Check the release schedule and never be in the channel during a release (Jim Falls' old channel takes scheduled whitewater releases).

Bigger-picture law

  • Wisconsin's 2017 repeal of the "Prove It First" law ended the effective sulfide-mining moratorium. A 2025–26 bill on sulfide permits (SB 623 / AB 632) failed on March 23, 2026, so the 2017 rules still stand.
  • Much of northern Wisconsin is in the 1837 and 1842 Ojibwe ceded territories, where tribes keep hunting, fishing and gathering rights. Tribes have opposed Reef, Crandon and Back Forty.
  • Burial mounds, graves and cemeteries are protected by Wisconsin's burial-sites law and are left off every map in this project on purpose.
Chapter 6: Key places by state

The closest real gold country to Eau Claire is the Chippewa Valley itself (glacial flour gold) and, an hour north, the Ladysmith volcanic belt. The richest historic lode districts are Ishpeming, Michigan and the Vermilion and Rainy Lake areas of Minnesota.

Near Eau Claire

SpotWhat to know
Dells Dam bedrock, Eau ClaireFlour gold in bedrock cracks and moss below the dam
Chippewa Falls, Jim Falls, Cornell (Brunet Falls), HolcombeBedrock below falls and dams on the Chippewa
Big Falls gold shaft (1896)Historic shaft on the Eau Claire River
Lake Hallie, Half Moon Lake, Wissota terraceOld Chippewa channels and outwash terraces
Seevers Creek, Dovre (1948)Gold confirmed by the University of Wisconsin
Rock Elm Creek, Pierce County (1887–1890)Worked placer creek
Town of Lucas well (1903)Well sand reported at $145 a ton

Wisconsin's deposits (the proof)

DepositCountyMetalsStatus
FlambeauRuskCopper, gold, silverMined 1993–1997, reclaimed; trails open, no collecting

Other Wisconsin reports: Omro gold mine (1873), Kirby Hills near Athelstane, Taylor County mining crews (1887), the Douglas County gold rush recollections, and Driftless reports at Avalanche and north of Prairie du Chien.

Minnesota

  • Lake Vermilion gold rush (1865): the state's first rush; Gold Island and Cook–Tower till surveys sit in the same belt.
  • Rainy Lake (1893): gold discovery and the Little American mine near Rainy Lake City.
  • Oronoco (1858): sluicing on the Zumbro River; also Rochester reports. Oronoco Park is a popular panning spot.
  • Modern drilling: Newmont (1985–1992), Gold Fields at Ely (1980), Vermillion Gold near Virginia and in Itasca County (2009–2022), and AngloGold Ashanti in Itasca and Koochiching counties (2017–2019).
  • Panning: North Shore creeks and the Lester River area (the only Lake Superior shore where hand panning is legal), the Vermilion River near Cook, the Big Fork near Effie, the Snake and Kettle rivers.

Michigan

  • Ropes Gold Mine, Ishpeming: Julius Ropes found gold in 1881; it is Michigan's best-known gold producer and was reopened in the 1980s. The atlas pin now sits on the water-filled pit and rock piles west of Deer Lake.
  • Michigan Gold Mine and Gold Mine Creek / Dead River near Ishpeming.
  • Douglass Houghton's "quill of gold" (1845) and Jacob Houghton's gold in native copper (1846) are the earliest Michigan reports.
  • Back Forty (Menominee County): a gold-rich zinc deposit with a long permit fight.
  • Lower Michigan: 1906 placer reports on the Grand, Muskegon, Manistee, Boyne, White and Rapid rivers; the gold is glacial, from Ontario. Barkus Campground is a pay-to-dig site.
Chapter 7: Chippewa Valley prospect spots

Every stream within an hour of Eau Claire reworks glacial drift that carries a little flour gold; the trick is finding the places that concentrate it. These 16 spots are ranked by evidence: documented gold first, then bedrock and black-sand traps, then unexplored ideas. Drive times are rough, from downtown Eau Claire, and several pins come from township-section records, so check a topo or satellite map before you go.

Documented gold

1. Plum Creek and Rock Elm Creek (Nugget Lake County Park, Rock Elm, Pierce Co.; about 70 min). The best-documented placer in the region. Flour gold was panned and sluiced commercially in 1887–1890, more than a dozen small diamonds turned up in the sluices, and a 1985 Superior Oil program confirmed placer gold without finding its source. Mindat lists gold, platinum, garnet, topaz and magnetite. The creek sits on the Rock Elm meteorite impact structure. How: ask Pierce County Parks about panning in the park; work Plum Creek below the dam and the Rock Elm tributaries on private land with permission, concentrating on gravel resting on sandstone.

2. Big Falls and Little Falls (Eau Claire River, Big Falls County Park, T27N R8W S13; about 20 min). A shaft or test pit was sunk mid-river here (records say 1896 and 1930), and gold was reportedly recovered from bedrock crevices. The river drops over ancient amphibolite gneiss and schist. How: county rules ban disturbing rocks in the park, so get written permission before crevicing, or work the corridor downstream toward County QQ with landowner permission. Nearby access: Highway D Landing (gravel beach under the bridge), Hobbs Landing at the Eau Claire–Chippewa confluence, Porterville Landing bars.

3. Snyder Park creeks (Town of Hewett, Clark Co.; about 65 min). The Wausau GPAA chapter held a club panning outing here in 2011, and Clark County has a historic assay of trace gold in a quartz vein with magnetite and arsenopyrite. How: call Clark County Forestry and Parks (715-743-5140) and ask the Wausau club which stream they worked.

4. Knapp shaft area (south of Knapp, Dunn Co., T28N R14W S16; about 40 min). WGNHS records a shaft possibly dug for alluvial gold; 1909 assays showed low gold and silver, and Knapp mining shares were sold locally. How: find the creek draining section 16 and test-pan its bars with permission. Low priority, but probably unpanned for decades.

5. Lowes Creek (Hwy 37 crossing, south Eau Claire; about 10 min). Old reports describe an adit, now cemented shut, with rumored gold and silver in the Mount Simon sandstone. How: mostly county park; scout only, with permission.

6. Black River at Neillsville (Neillsville–Granton area, Clark Co.; about 65 min). Gold was rumored in the basal conglomerate of the Mount Simon sandstone, a fossil placer laid on Precambrian rock half a billion years ago. How: look where the river or O'Neill Creek exposes sandstone on granite or gneiss; sample the pebbly base and the gravel just downstream.

Bedrock and black-sand traps

7. Jim Falls old channel (Chippewa River below the dam, T30N R7W S30; about 35 min). The dam bypasses the original channel, leaving amphibolite, granite and pegmatite exposed most of the year. A magnetic high runs east-southeast from the falls. How: work crevices and potholes at low flow; check the whitewater release schedule and never be in the channel during a release.

8. Below Holcombe Dam (T32N R6W S28; about 55 min). Bedrock outcrops below the dam, and the Flambeau and Jump join just upstream; the Flambeau drains the Flambeau mine country. How: sample crevices and the first slow water; scout the flowage shoreline gravel during the late-winter drawdown (up to 10 ft).

9. Cornell rapids (T31N R6W S18; about 45 min). Precambrian rock in the river, near where the Chippewa lobe stopped. How: crevices and bars below the dam; Brunet Island State Park is DNR land, so ask about a collector's permit there.

10. Lake Arbutus Dam outcrop (Black River at Hatfield, T22N R3W S3; about 60 min). One of the largest exposures of Archean rock in Wisconsin, the Hatfield Gneiss, more than 2.5 billion years old, running about 0.6 mile downstream: a long natural riffle. How: crevice at low water and respect the dam safety zone.

11. Black River Falls rapids (about 55 min). The gneiss forms a long rapid and then disappears under sandstone, so heavies settle out; the Iron Mound iron formation just upstream should make the black sand rich. How: first bars below the rapid, inside bends, behind boulders; strip the magnetite with a magnet and check what is left.

12. Popple–Black confluence (Hwy 73, Town of Warner, Clark Co.; about 65 min). The rivers join over Precambrian rock, with Class I–II rapids and about a dozen bedrock ledges down to Greenwood County Park. How: paddle or wade the stretch at low water, sampling each ledge.

Unexplored ideas

13. Iron Mound black-sand streams (around Wazee Lake, the old Jackson County Iron Mine; about 60 min). The taconite pit was cut into iron formation averaging about 35% magnetite with garnet; its streams should carry the heaviest black sand around. How: streams draining the mounds outside the recreation area, with permission.

14. Eau Claire River forks (east of Augusta, T26N R5W S29; about 35 min). The Eau Claire Volcanic Complex here is the same age as the belt that hosts Flambeau, and its mineral potential is poorly understood. How: pan the confluence and both forks and compare with Big Falls downstream.

15. Yellow River below Gilman (Taylor and Chippewa Co.; about 70 min). The Bend copper-gold deposit lies a few hundred yards from the Yellow north of Gilman, but it is buried under 100–120 ft of glacial sediment. Speculative. How: look for bars between Gilman and Cadott and map where colors appear.

16. Lower Chippewa outwash bars (Caryville to Durand; about 40 min). The Chippewa was the Chippewa lobe's main meltwater channel and still cuts that fill; gold rides thin black-sand layers on bar heads after floods. How: stay off State Natural Area land; big volumes and a matting sluice suit this gold.

Old river channels near Eau Claire

A height-above-river model of the valley shows abandoned channels just above today's river: O1, a meander loop below Chippewa Falls; O2, the low terrace at Lake Hallie; O3, the Wissota terrace toward Bloomer; O4, meander scars in the Caryville bottoms; O5, Half Moon Lake, a cut-off loop; O6, a meltwater valley into the Yellow River at Cadott. When a river moves, its heavy bottom gravel stays behind under a few feet of sand or silt. Glacial landmarks from Syverson's Chippewa County bulletin: the Chippewa and Jump River diversion channels at Cornell and Holcombe, the Otter Lake tunnel channel and esker (a natural sluice), the Chippewa Moraine boulder country, the Perkinstown moraine front, and the Bob Lake ice-walled-lake delta.

The Chippewa gold trail test

The most likely theory of all (about 70% in the research notes) is that ice and the Chippewa carried belt rock past Big Falls toward Eau Claire. The test is simple: pan equal volumes at five spots from Eau Claire to Cornell and compare color counts. Sharp-edged grains point to a nearby source.

Chapter 8: Wisconsin's gold belt: deposits, targets and theories

The best odds for new gold sit along the shear zones and volcanic districts around Wisconsin's known deposits, where thick glacial cover hid bedrock from past explorers. This chapter is the big-picture research from the Wisconsin target work; rankings and odds are judgment calls from public data, not proven resources.

Who is exploring now (2026)

ProjectOwnerStatus

Reef (Marathon Co.) goldGreenLight MetalsNo drilling; a 2022 notice was withdrawn as incomplete

Crandon (Forest Co.)Mole Lake Ojibwe and Forest County Potawatomi since 2003No mining
Back Forty (Michigan)Gold Resource Corp.Permits contested for years

On paper (old, non-compliant estimates, gold about $4,166/oz in Oct 2026): Reef, 454,000 tons at about 0.26–0.31 oz/ton, roughly 119,000–140,000 oz ($495–582 million in the ground). Bend, about 311,000 oz in two zones (roughly $1.3 billion). These are gross metal values, not profit.

Ranked target areas

RankAreaCountiesStyleAnchor evidence
1Reef shear corridorMarathonShear-hosted (orogenic) quartz-sulfide veinsNoranda estimate ~454,000 tons at ~10.6 g/t; Aquila hit 65.2 m at 2.80 g/t

Florence County: the newest lead

Re-scoring with the 2025 USGS airborne magnetics, about 3,100 USGS soil, stream and till samples, 1 m LiDAR and the state core inventory moved Florence County to the top. Magnetic highs H8, H6 and H1 each carry three or more clues; around H8, glacial till runs up to 79 ppm arsenic (normal about 4) and 11 ppm antimony, a classic pairing near orogenic gold. The targets sit on the Niagara suture, the boundary between the Pembine–Wausau volcanic arc and the old continental margin, and big sutures are where orogenic gold collects. USGS Professional Paper 633 (1971) adds target FS (about 45.827, −88.228): drill holes in slate with pyrrhotite and pyrite veinlets beside an unexplained 6,750-gamma magnetic peak. Minatome cored 14 holes near H8, and that core is still in the state library.

LiDAR found dug-looking pits (13–22 m wide, 1.2–2.9 m deep, most with spoil piles). Best Florence candidates: P1 (45.80992, −88.14017; WI DNR land), P3 (45.80289, −88.16794), P5 (45.87765, −88.29259; maybe a road borrow pit) and P6 (45.79704, −88.15644). Florence was heavily prospected for iron, so some pits may be iron test pits, whose dumps are still free bedrock samples.

Also high: Flambeau at Ladysmith (11), Wisconsin River at Wausau (14) and the Pelican River (14 after the 1985 state list). The historic placer streams Plum Creek, Rock Elm Creek and Big Falls rank just outside the top 20 because their gold is glacial flour, not from a nearby lode. Typical low water (USGS gauges 2014–2026): late August to September everywhere; the Pine runs 260–290 cfs then against a 1,050 cfs April peak.

Six theories

TheoryKey evidenceFirst testOdds of a first-test hit
Chippewa Valley gold trail to Eau ClaireIce and river carried belt rock past Big FallsPan equal volumes at five spots, Eau Claire to Cornell~70%
Wausau telluride gold districtReef, the Eason 200-ft shaft, calaverite in Wausau pegmatite, Mosinee gold, NE faultsTellurium, gold and arsenic in stream silt~55%

The Price–Lincoln chain (USGS records)

Prentice East (zinc), Ritchie Creek (bornite, chalcocite, chalcopyrite, electrum, gold, tetrahedrite), Spirit (base metals), Hawk (electrum, but gold not listed as a commodity) and Horseshoe (gold, silver, polybasite). Hawk and Horseshoe were logged as zinc-copper prospects even though gold minerals were seen: exactly the gold earlier explorers weren't chasing. Mole Lake and Catwillow in Forest County also list gold as a byproduct.

Bedrock windows (mostly parks, look only)

Dells of the Eau Claire County Park (gorge on the Reef shear zone, 45.006, −89.337); Big Falls County Park; Big Falls of the Jump River at Kennan (between Flambeau and Bend); Twelve Foot Falls and Long Slide Falls (Pembine area, near the Archie veins); Rib Mountain State Park (quartzite above the Wausau plain).

Lore, cross-checked

Of 23 old stories, the four most credible sit near Wausau or have modern confirmation: the Eason 200-ft shaft (now the Reef prospect), Wausau pegmatite gold (calaverite), the Mosinee localities, and Plum Creek. Stories in southern sandstone or dolomite (Prairie du Chien, the McDougal farm, Knapp stock) score lowest. Also worth chasing: the Penokee Gap camp (Chicago Mine, Northern Belle and Brunschweiler Creek, worked only 1879–81).

Wild cards

  • The Rock Elm meteorite crater (6.5 km) beside Plum Creek as a home for Plum Creek's missing source.
  • Cambrian beach placers in the basal Mount Simon sandstone, which sits directly on the belt's eroded edge.
  • Deposits under the sandstone edge: Flambeau sat under a sandstone caprock that preserved a rich weathered zone about 300 ft deep.
  • Railroad land grants: Bend's mineral rights belong to the Soo Line Railroad, so old grants may hold other belt mineral rights.
  • Twig chemistry, lake-bottom mud cores and well arsenic data as cheap regional screens.
  • Meteorites are not a gold source (only about 0.1–4 ppm gold). Wisconsin has two impact structures (Rock Elm, Glover Bluff) and 14 recorded meteorites; Brussels Hill in Door County is the leading candidate for a third.
Chapter 9: Gold reports and rushes

These are the real reports behind the map pins, from state surveys and old newspapers. Most were small or short-lived, a few were false alarms, and the cluster west of Eau Claire sits on the red Lake Superior drift (Chapter 3). Treat dollar values as the old claims they are.

Wisconsin: around Eau Claire

  • Big Falls gold shaft, Eau Claire River (1896). A 1965 Daily Telegram history column says gold operations flourished in the Eau Claire area in 1896, with a 30-foot shaft sunk into a hill at Big Falls and worked for some time; a later test ran about $20 a ton. The 1985 state list adds a rumored 1930 pit mid-river in bedrock crevices.
  • Gold south of Durand (1800s). The same column reports gold on the south side of Durand, on the Chippewa below Eau Claire.
  • Seevers Creek, town of Dovre (1948). Clayton A. Seevers, 55, announced at the Barron County courthouse that he had panned gold in a creek on the Solberg farm near New Auburn and filed a 40-acre claim. A University of Wisconsin metallurgist confirmed the gold, and two other prospectors staked claims nearby.
  • Knapp (1901). Residents had found gold while digging on their land; Sam Tufts sent a panful of dirt to Minneapolis that assayed about $3 a ton with silver and copper.
  • Town of Lucas well, near Menomonie (1903). Rock from five-foot intervals over 85 feet of a well, mixed and assayed, ran $145 a ton.
  • Eau Galle gold mine (early 1900s). Gold was found, shares were sold to many local residents, and the mine did not pay.
  • Dunn County (1902). The Wisconsin Blue Book chronology lists a Dunn County gold find in October 1902, making Dunn the most-reported gold county in the newspaper uploads.
  • Heinenman's shaft, Pepin (1909). Farmer F.O. Heinenman, caught up in a local prospecting craze, sank a 40-foot shaft and claimed ore worth over $150 a ton in copper, gold and silver.
  • Plum Creek shaft (1890s). About 2,000 acres around Plum Creek were optioned; a 15-foot shaft below creek level found quartz crystals, graphite, mica, magnetic iron and traces of gold and platinum. Rock Elm and Plum creeks were worked as placers in 1887–1890, and small diamonds turned up in the sluices.
  • The Barlow farm nugget, south of Hudson (1906). One of George Steckmeyer's children found a gold nugget on the Barlow farm about eight miles south of Hudson, and the gold excitement in the region was "greatly intensified" (Wausau Pilot).
  • River Falls well sands (1906). Gold-bearing sand in an old well led to a $330,000 offer for a 225-acre farm that had sold three years earlier for $13,000.
  • Polk County (1902). A Blue Book gold report from August 1902, on the copper-bearing volcanics near St. Croix Falls.
  • St. Croix Dalles (about 1890). The region's only documented placer production: flakes and scales in cracks of the trap rock, worked at low water.

Wisconsin: the north and east

  • Taylor County mining crews (1887). The Chippewa Falls Herald, quoting the Medford Star and News, said crews were engaged at Chelsea, Medford and Pine Creek and expected ore before the snow; Chas. Powell brought in quartz with free gold and claimed to know the ledge.
  • Penokee Gap (1879–81). The Chicago Mine and Northern Belle worked gold, copper and silver briefly; Brunschweiler Creek saw a placer attempt in the 1880s.
  • Holmes Mining & Milling, near Mellen (1902). Shafts of 150 and 188 ft, a 40-ft gossan traceable half a mile, assays to $3 gold and 9 oz silver a ton.
  • Chippewa mine, Douglas County. Gold in diabase ledges, $2 to $11 a ton (Crane, 1908).
  • Northern Clark County. Gold and silver in quartz with pyrite and arsenopyrite, the only northern bedrock gold the early state survey confirmed.
  • Kirby Hills, Athelstane (1910). Homesteader Michael Smith claimed a Philadelphia mint assay of $12 gold and $3 silver a ton, 20 miles north of Marinette.
  • "Badger Gold Found in Fowl" (about 1901). A Vilas County News headline: gold in a chicken or goose crop means the gravel the bird ate held gold.
  • Douglas County gold rush recollections (1925 story). "Old timers tell about rush for Wisconsin gold," naming John A. Bardon and George R. Stuntz.
  • Emmet mine (1879). Gold found in iron ore; a short-lived excitement, location unknown.

Wisconsin: the south (treat with caution)

  • Omro (1873). Gold reported in quartz about 60 ft down near a railroad cut four miles north of Omro.
  • Stockbridge (1903). George Howe picked up a rock that fell from a gravel wagon; it tested at $20 a ton.
  • Sussex (1900). August Nemitz's farm quartz and gravel assayed $6.33 and $8.95 a ton.
  • Lake Como (1931). A Chicago man digging a cottage post hole found sand a jeweler guessed at $800 a ton.
  • J.V. Allen farm, Avalanche (1901) and Dousman "gold quartz" near Prairie du Chien (1902): both in the Driftless Area on limestone country, most likely pyrite.
  • Kaukauna "fool's gold" (1919): a reported find that turned out to be pyrite, the classic false alarm.

Minnesota

  • Oronoco and Rochester (1858). The Rochester Democrat described 90 to 100 men at the Oronoco diggings earning two to six dollars a day each; gold turned up in the Zumbro at both towns that summer. Oronoco still holds Gold Rush Days every August.
  • Lake Vermilion gold rush (1865–1868). State Geologist Henry Eames had a quartz vein assayed at $23 a ton; rumor grew it to $900. The rush town of Winston reached about 300 people and was abandoned by fall 1868. Gold Island got its name in that rush; the gold proved too lean.
  • Rainy Lake (1893). George Davis and Charles Moore found a gold-bearing quartz vein in July 1893; Duluth investors started the Little American Mine in January 1894, and Rainy Lake City (about 500 people, a bank, hotels, a newspaper and a jail) was abandoned by 1901.
  • Mud Creek till anomaly (2005). DNR Report 365: four of 32 basal-till samples over the Vermilion greenstone held 88 to 1,282 gold grains per 10 kg, up to 98% sharp-edged (barely moved), with bedrock grabs to 12,247 ppb gold.
  • Cook–Tower till survey (2012–2017). About 216 till samples found five small high-grain clusters in 2012 (three in never-explored ground) and an 18-sample cluster confirmed in 2017 at Murray Road South.
  • Modern drilling. Newmont (1985–1992), Gold Fields at Ely (1980), Vermillion Gold near Virginia and in Itasca County (2009–2022) and AngloGold Ashanti (about 180 holes, 2017–2019).
  • Mize cousins, Kittson County (1878). A tale of $25,000 panned near Two Rivers, with no source and geology against it.
  • Delhi, McFarland Lake and Old Spaulding: USGS gold records in hornfels and slate.

Michigan

  • Douglass Houghton's quill of gold (1845). The state geologist reportedly found rock near Negaunee with enough free gold to fill an eagle's quill, told only Samuel Worth Hill, and drowned in Lake Superior that October. The spot was lost.
  • Jacob Houghton (1846). A native copper vein with a little gold: a 28-ounce specimen yielded 12 grains.
  • Silas Smith (1854–55) claimed gold and silver inside Marquette; later finds backed him up.
  • Silver Lake district (1864–1868). Assayers found economic gold in pyrite northwest of Ishpeming; over 35 companies formed and none reported gold production.
  • Cascade Iron Company vein, Palmer (1869). Assays to $900 a ton, too small to mine.
  • Ropes Gold Mine (1881). Marquette chemist Julius Ropes found a gold-bearing quartz vein outside Ishpeming on May 17, 1881. The mine ran about 15 years with some 35 men, produced roughly $645,792 to over $700,000 in gold and silver (about 80% gold) and never paid a dividend. It was reopened in the 1980s; the pit and rock piles sit west of Deer Lake.
  • Michigan Gold Mine (1880s–1890s). Pilfering was so bad the company fenced the property and searched every worker; two miners were caught with $3,000 in gold just before leaving for Europe.
  • Grummett prospect, Michigamme (1906–1913): showed free gold but found no buyers.
  • Lower Peninsula placers (1906). The State Board of Geological Survey listed placer gold on the Grand, Muskegon, Manistee, Boyne, White, Rapid and Little Sable rivers, Lowell and Ada Creek, and near Marcellus and Burr Oak. All glacial, from Ontario; some was authenticated and some may have been pyrite.
Chapter 10: Treasure tales

Each story is tagged by how reliable it is: documented (court, government or museum records), newspaper, legend (long-told, no record) or rumor (a forum post or an uncited web article). Most treasure legends are just that; the documented ones are where the history is real. Burial mounds, graves and cemeteries are never searched.

Close to Eau Claire

  • Kraft State Bank robbery, Menomonie (1931; documented). On October 20, 1931 the Holden-Keating gang robbed the Kraft State Bank of more than $90,000 in cash and securities and took hostages. They fled east on U.S. 12, north on County Trunk B, then east on old Suckow Road, spreading nails behind them, and stashed gas at abandoned farms where they left a dying member with some of the securities. No source says the money was recovered. About 25 minutes away.
  • Neillsville silver jar (1962; documented, found). Frederick Wagner, digging a ditch, broke open a pint fruit jar inside a pail 18 inches down, 3 miles west of Neillsville: $56.30 in 1800s silver dimes through dollars. Farm caches usually look exactly like this.
  • Muddy Creek fence-line gold, Elk Mound (rumor). $35,000 in gold coins supposedly buried along a fence line whose wooden posts were later replaced with metal. No source found; a gravel pit sits nearby.
  • Hurlburt's hidden money, Rush River valley (1899; rumor). Wealthy farmer Benjamin Hurlburt was said to hide money in the woods; only about $195 was in his estate.
  • Whitehall treasure cave (1924; newspaper). "Whitehall barber guards famous treasure cave" (Milwaukee Journal), naming T.J. Johnson; likely a fur-trade story.
  • French gold at the Black River forks, Hatfield (rumor). A bag of gold artifacts said to be reburied at the East Fork junction. Note: if any story involves a mound, it is a burial site and off limits.
  • Nelson bluff caves, Buffalo County (legend). Soldiers' treasure in small bluff caves; no finds recorded.
  • Spanish gold of Lake Pepin (legend, both shores). Late-1700s Spanish traders' gold; no source. The real history here is Fort Saint Antoine, a French post of 1686.
  • Lake City bootleggers' caches (legend). A bootlegger who buried cash and died in a car crash; across Lake Pepin, about 1 hour 20 minutes.
  • Winona Gang loot (legend). "Big Frank" Connors' 1880s gang supposedly buried train and store loot around Winona.

Northwest Wisconsin and the Apostle Islands

  • Capone's Hideout, Cranberry Lake, Sawyer County (legend). The stone lodge and guard tower are real; the machine-gun turret, floatplane whiskey runs and hidden money are legend.
  • Battaglan stolen silver, Sawyer County (1924; legend, partly found). Martha Battaglan hid $11,200 in stolen silver coins; police recovered some in St. Paul and her father found $3,000 near Beaver Lake.
  • Montana gold wagon, Polk County (legend). $200,000 in bullion lost in a swamp seven miles northeast of St. Croix Falls.
  • St. Croix fur traders' gold (legend). Gold and jewelry buried while fleeing an attack; searchers have looked near Taylors Falls.
  • James Becker's bonds, Glidden (1893; legend). $50,000 in government bonds hidden in the woods; 15 cents ever recovered.
  • Eli Pingers' gold, La Pointe (1861; newspaper). $35,000 buried, per an 1897 New York Times story.
  • Hermit Island (legend). William Wilson hid about $91,000 in coins before dying in 1861; older tales add a pirate cave, and quarry owner Frederick Prentice is also said to have buried money.
  • York Island iron box (1760) and Sand Island silver chest (1778): British soldiers' caches (legends).
  • Stockton Island thieves' cache (legend). Nuggets, ore and stolen goods. All Apostle Islands land is national lakeshore: look only.

Elsewhere in Wisconsin

  • Dillinger's suitcase, Little Bohemia (1934; legend). After the April 1934 FBI raid, Dillinger supposedly buried a suitcase of $200,000 or more about 500 yards behind the lodge. The raid is real; an FBI interview suggests he still had the suitcase about 10 days later.
  • Fort Crawford payroll (1832; legend). Four saddlebags of gold coins, $20,000 each, said buried on the highest bluff near Prairie du Chien during the Black Hawk War.
  • The lost gold of Brisbois (1924 story; newspaper). Prairie du Chien fur trader Michel Brisbois (died 1837) and an heiress to his gold.
  • Wisconsin River bluff cave, Richland County (1923; newspaper). Possibly Bogus Bluff, the 1828 counterfeiters' cave near Gotham.
  • Wildcat Mountain (legend). A Montana gold wagon, or James-Younger loot.
  • Riverboat gold bars, Portage (rumor). An 1870 wreck with $100,000 aboard; three 10-lb bars said found in 1953.
  • R.C. Bennett's tin boxes, Vilas County (legend, partly found). About $40,000 in coins in 60 tin boxes; his wife found some after his death in 1950.
  • Crivitz hill (1917; newspaper), Crazy Man's Island, Okauchee Lake (legend) and Sheridan Park beach coins, Milwaukee (legend) round out the list.

Minnesota

  • Hamm kidnapping ransom (1933; documented). The Barker-Karpis gang took brewer William Hamm Jr.; the $100,000 ransom was paid on Highway 61 north of Wyoming. No one knows if it was spent or cached.
  • Bremer kidnapping ransom (1934; newspaper). The same gang collected $200,000 for banker Edward Bremer; investigators believed part was buried by a fence post between Rochester and Chatfield (Highway 52 or 42, depending on the telling). More than $100,000 was unaccounted for.
  • Old Soldiers' Home gold, Minneapolis (documented). A deathbed story of Civil War-era gold led the 1943 legislature to pass a law (House File 934, Chapter 357) letting a seeker dig on state grounds. Apparently nothing was found.
  • Le Sueur's lost mine and Fort L'Huillier (1700–1702; documented, partly). Pierre Le Sueur dug blue-green earth he thought was copper ore and shipped 4,000 lb to France; the fort site was found in 1907, the mine cave never.
  • James-Younger loot, Northfield (1876; legend). Historians agree the gang got almost nothing from the bank, so the cache probably never existed.
  • Hinckley payroll (1894; legend). A lumber company's gold payroll said lost in the fire that killed over 400 people.
  • Also told: Old Sherburne's $40,000 and an 1862 payroll in Sherburne County, Charles Ney's brewery fortune and the Curran brothers' $40,000 in Sibley County, Joseph Winther's gold coins (Faribault), H. Lilly's $60,000 at La Crescent, bandits' coins west of Wadena (1890), Thomas Fontaine's missing cash (Polk County, 1904), William Colvill's gold near Grand Marais, Red River coins near Noyes, and French traders' silver at Lake Vermilion (silver really was found on Gold Island in 1865).

Michigan

  • Michigan Gold Mine pilfered gold (newspaper). Thousands of dollars stolen by miners; the total was never known.
  • Confederate gold in Lake Michigan (legend). Gold from Jefferson Davis's baggage train, said lost in a storm on a railcar ferry; the subject of the TV series Curse of Civil War Gold.
  • Uncited web legends (treat as entertainment): Capone's loot near Hermansville or Escanaba, Fayette townsite money (a state historic site: no detecting), the lost Ontonagon silver mine (about 1820), Grayling train gold, King Strang's Beaver Island treasure, and Whitefish Point shipwreck valuables (underwater preserve: look only).
Chapter 11: Ghost towns and detecting sites

Coins and relics pile up wherever people gathered, waited, worked or swam for decades. Every site here needs the landowner's permission, and Wisconsin DNR land allows detecting only to find a specific lost item, with a permit.
