CCC camps (1933–1941)

Camps Globe and Fairchild (Fairchild), Nelson, Perkinstown, Mondeaux and Rusk in Wisconsin, plus Rabideau, Cusson, Lanesboro and Big Lake (Cloquet) in Minnesota. Each held about 200 men. Find the barracks rows on 1938 aerial photos and the camp dump in a nearby ravine.

Vanished settlements

  • Wisconsin, near home: Nelsonville, Oak Grove and Porter's Mills (Eau Claire Co.); Old Tyrone and Welch Point (Dunn); Kurth and Trow (Clark); Charter Oak Mills, Clay and Wrightsville (Jackson); Cortland, New City and Williamsburg (Trempealeau); Anchorage and Bohri (Buffalo). Old store, school, mill and house sites are where coins and tokens collect.
  • Wisconsin north: Star Lake logging town (1890s–1930s); the Hurley saloon district (1890s–1930s).
  • Minnesota: Winston (the 1866 Lake Vermilion rush town); Rainy Lake City (1894–1901 gold boomtown); Nininger (Ignatius Donnelly's 1856 boom town, emptied by the Panic of 1857, about an hour away); Point Douglas (1850s river town; the county park beach allows permit detecting); Elcor (Mesabi) and Manganese (Cuyuna) mining towns; and Belden, Bodum, Cazenovia, Constance, Coopers Corner, Cuba, Fairland, Harlis, London, Pitt, West Newton and Withrow.
  • Michigan copper country: Central (1850s–1898), Delaware, Mandan, the Kearsarge–Allouez strip of six miners' towns, Nonesuch (about 300 people, a baseball team), Old Victoria, Old White Pine, the Rockland mine townsites, Silver City, Donken and Calderwood (partly under the Bond Falls Flowage). Fayette is a state historic site: no detecting.

Amusement parks and landings in Minnesota

Wildwood Amusement Park (1889–1938), Big Island Park on Lake Minnetonka (1906–1911), Excelsior Amusement Park and ferry terminal (1925–1973), and the Oronoco Gold Rush Days fairgrounds.

Beaches with detecting rules

  • Minnesota county parks such as Square Lake, Big Marine, St. Croix Bluffs, Lake Byllesby, Schulze Lake (Lebanon Hills) and Point Douglas are county or regional park beaches; some, like Point Douglas, allow detecting with a permit, so check each park's rules. Park Point in Duluth is a long Lake Superior beach. Minnesota state parks ban detectors.
  • Michigan state parks allow detecting only in designated areas: Baraga, Bewabic, Brimley, Craig Lake, Lake Gogebic, Twin Lakes, Van Riper and the Porcupine Mountains have such areas; F.J. McLain allows rock picking but not detecting. Black River Harbor is in the Ottawa National Forest.
Chapter 12: Copper, agates and Lake Superior

Lake Superior country trades gold for native copper, silver and agates, and the collecting rules are stricter on the shore than inland.

Float copper

  • Native copper from the Keweenaw rift was plucked by glaciers and dropped south as "float copper" across northern Wisconsin and Minnesota. A detector is the best tool; nuggets often sit in plowed fields and gravel pits.
  • Wisconsin's record-style finds include a 15 lb nugget near Ellsworth.
  • Half-breeds are copper and silver fused together, prized by collectors.

Record float copper

FindWhereSize
Houghton County airport massHoughton Co., MI (early 2000s)About 35 tons, the largest known; cut up and smelted
Quincy claims massNear Boston Location, north of Hancock (1997)26.6 tons; the largest that still exists (Collector's Edge, Golden, CO)
Ontonagon BoulderWest Branch of the Ontonagon RiverKnown to Native people long before Schoolcraft (1820) and Douglass Houghton (1831); removed 1843, now at the Smithsonian
Sioux River boulderBayfield Co., WI1,700 lb, Wisconsin's biggest recorded in Lake Superior country
Pella nuggetShawano Co., WI970 lb

Minnesota's Mineral Heritage bulletin records copper boulders of hundreds of pounds in Chisago and Pine county drift. Any Superior- or Green Bay-lobe drift can hold float copper, though it thins out southward. The Dresser trap rock quarry (Polk Co.) and the Montreal River gorge show native copper in its home basalt, and more than a dozen old Douglas County copper workings sit on the Douglas Range (the Weyerhaeuser mine near Gordon reached 300 ft).

Copper country stops

  • A.E. Seaman Mineral Museum (Michigan Tech): learn what float copper, datolite and silver look like first, and get Keweenaw Mineral Days dates, when rock piles at Seneca, Wolverine, Central and Baltic are flipped for collectors with permission.
  • Central Mine rock piles: open for picking only when gates are closed and no work is underway.
  • Coles Creek, the Hancock gravel quarry outwash and even the Michigan Tech campus have produced float copper.
  • Prospector's Paradise rock bins on US-41 at Allouez: a reliable rainy-day stop.
  • Susie Island near Pigeon Point, MN: copper veins explored with a shaft; no ore shipped.

Keweenaw rock piles

  • Old mine rock piles hold copper, silver, datolite and other minerals. Most are private; the Cliff mine piles are the big Keweenaw pile that's legal to pick and detect.
  • Michigan's 25 lb a year limit applies on state and public trust land.

Prehistoric copper mining (look only)

  • People mined Keweenaw and Isle Royale copper thousands of years ago with stone hammers. Isle Royale holds more than 1,000 ancient pits, about 4,500 years old.
  • The pit districts show where copper reached the surface, which is why they're on the map at area level. They are protected and never to be disturbed.

Lake Superior beaches

  • Lake Superior agates wash up on gravel beaches and river mouths; black sand (magnetite) streaks mark heavy-mineral beaches.
  • Minnesota's North Shore is the only Lake Superior shore where hand panning is legal. Wisconsin bans collecting on the state-owned lakebed, and Michigan closes Great Lakes shores and bottomlands to panning.
  • The Porcupine Mountains are copper country, not gold country; Black River Harbor and the Presque Isle River are scenic, look-first spots in the Ottawa National Forest.
  • Silver City (near the Porkies) had a short silver boom.
Chapter 13: History timeline and tidbits

Regional gold history runs from prehistoric copper miners through two small 1800s rushes to modern company drilling, newest first below.

WhenWhat happened

Tidbits worth remembering

  • Most of the 1800s "rushes" faded within a few years; the gold was real but too fine or too scattered to pay.
  • Gold in Wisconsin is usually flour-size and rides with black sand.
  • The Kaukauna "gold" turned out to be fool's gold, a classic false alarm.
  • A modern explorer only drills after mapping, sampling and geophysics point to something, so drill clusters are the best public hint of what pros believed.
  • The atlas also carries treasure stories (caches, robbery loot, payrolls, pilfered mine gold) and detecting sites (CCC camps, ghost towns, fairgrounds, drive-ins, landings); see those layers for each story.
Chapter 14: Reading the data

The atlas layers several data sets; each answers a different question, and none of them sees gold directly.

DataWhat it showsHow to read it
1 m LiDAR (USGS 3DEP)Bare ground under the treesReddish = raised (rock piles, mounds); bluish = hollows (pits, shafts, trenches, cellar holes). Three or more hollows deeper than 2.5 m near a target hint at old workings
0.6 m aerial photo (USDA NAIP)What's on the surface nowBare rock, tailings, water-filled pits, roads; matches the LiDAR square
Magnetic anomaly map (USGS)Iron-rich and volcanic rock, even under driftRed = magnetic highs, blue = lows; sharp edges mark contacts and faults
Stream-sediment chemistry (USGS)Gold and arsenic in creek mudHigh arsenic is a pathfinder for gold
Geologic maps (USGS SGMC)Which rock is under the driftGreenstone and volcanic units are the gold hosts
Depth to bedrock (MN Geological Survey, 2025)How deep the rock isUnder about 100 ft = drill-only; thin cover plus outcrops = workable
Drill core library (MN DNR)Where companies drilledClusters = professional targets
Sentinel-2 satellite indicesBare rock and iron-oxide colorWeak under forest; its "new" patches turned out to be fields and clear-cuts

The gold model

  • Built from geology, faults, magnetics and stream chemistry, then tested on known gold sites it never saw. Its score on that test is about 0.81, where 0.5 is a coin flip and 1.0 is perfect.
  • Its 30 model zones are untested ideas more than 10 km from known gold. Most Minnesota zones are buried under 250–970 ft of glacial sediment; zone 26 near the Mesabi Range has thin cover and 439 outcrops within 3 km.
  • Several zones landed within about 5–17 km of Newmont and Noranda drilling without the model knowing about it.
Chapter 15: Research toolkit: records, law, gear and people

The cheapest discoveries come from records other people already paid for: old company drill core, state filings, survey maps and newspapers. Start there, then go to the ground where two sources agree.

Records

RecordWhat it gives youHow to use it
Company drill data at the state (Wis. Stat. 107.15)Licensees file drill locations and rock logs; confidential only until Dec 31 of the third year after filing, and core is released within 10 years1970s–1990s data should now be public. Logs leave out metal minerals by law, so the core itself matters
WGNHS core repository, Mount HorebDecades of company coreIndustry access about $505 a day; portable XRF about $6.34 a sample. XRF is good for arsenic and copper but too insensitive for low gold, so send the best intervals for fire assay
MN DNR Drill Core Library, Hibbing, and MinarchiveLocations of 22,641 borings and scanned company reportsFind exploration holes near any Minnesota spot
WGNHS exploration summaries (1980–1987)Every licensed company and where it drilledAnomalies with no nearby holes are the real gaps
DNR mining projects pageCurrent drilling noticesGround near new drilling is worth a look
County LiDAR (WisconsinView, MnTOPO)5-ft and 1 m bare-earth elevationOld pits, trenches and shafts under forest
1800s land-survey notesTrees, soil and township descriptionsWeak for gold; good for old shorelines and outcrops
UW theses (MINDS@UW)Assays and logs for Lynne, Flambeau and ReefPull assay tables
Old newspapersForgotten finds and digsSearch "gold" with belt town names (Ladysmith, Medford, Prentice, Mellen, Wausau), 1870–1940; for 1902 Dunn and Polk finds try the Menomonie Dunn County News (Oct 1902) and St. Croix Falls or Osceola papers (Aug 1902)
Private-well arsenic data (DNR)Wells above 10 ppb arsenicA cheap regional sulfide screen

Ownership

  • Dormant mineral rights (Wis. Stat. 706.057): a severed mineral interest lapses to the surface owner after 20 years unused, unless a claim is recorded. Use means mining, recording a deal, paying taxes on it, or recording a statement of claim. A surface owner records a claim with the county register of deeds; it takes effect at lapse, is void after 6 years without one, and the mineral owner has 3 years to contest.
  • County tax-deed sales in Price and Taylor counties: check whether minerals were reserved before bidding.
  • Mineral rights are often split from the surface; check each parcel at the register of deeds. This is a summary, not legal advice; ask a Wisconsin real-estate attorney before acting.

Gear beyond the pan

ToolFindsStrengthsLimits
VLF-EMSteep conductive bodies such as sulfide lenses and faultsPassive (uses existing radio transmitters), cheap, quick line surveysShallow, fooled by fences, pipes and power lines
Ground magnetometerMagnetic rock and magnetic sulfides (pyrrhotite)Rentable; pairs with USGS magnetic gridsCrandon-type ore can be non-magnetic
Soil-gas samplingGases from buried sulfides through tillTested at CrandonNeeds a lab; varies with weather
Multi-element assay of silt or basal tillTellurium, arsenic, bismuth, antimony pathfindersFlags gold ground before gold showsLab cost

Practical order: walk VLF-EM lines across the strike of a target, mark conductors, then check them with a magnetometer and soil samples.

Pathfinder clues in the field

Rusty quartz with boxy holes where sulfides weathered out; rusty rock or black sand a magnet grabs (pyrrhotite, common in Reef ore); black sand with pink garnets; boulder trains of sulfide or vein quartz; orange seeps and dead patches; old square prospect pits (like the Gold Diggers Area pits, T40N R11E); and upturned tree roots and ant mounds, which bring deeper till to the surface for free.

People

  • Wausau Prospectors (GPAA chapter founded 2007, over 100 members): meets the first Saturday of each month at 11 AM; phone (715) 340-2831 or their Facebook page (their old website now shows spam).
  • Twin Cities Prospectors (GPAA): (612) 245-6569.
  • GPAA chapters also meet in Tomah and Greenbush.
  • Well drillers, quarry and gravel-pit operators and county foresters see bedrock, sulfides and rusty water first. Bring a printed map.
  • If a target tests well on ground you control, a junior company may pay to option it. GreenLight is the only company actively drilling the Wisconsin belt, and Badger Minerals still owns land at Schoepke.

Data services worth knowing

USGS MRDS (mineral records), USGS NGDB (geochemistry), the USGS magnetic grids and the 2025 Earth MRI airborne surveys, USGS 3DEP LiDAR, USDA NAIP aerial photos (0.6 m), the Minnesota Geospatial Commons and Minnesota Geological Survey open data, WGNHS services, and Microsoft Planetary Computer for aerials and satellite scenes. Satellite alteration mapping (Sentinel-2) failed under forest and glacial cover in every test; ground sampling is the way forward.

Chapter 16: Glossary
TermMeaning
Black sandHeavy dark minerals (mostly magnetite) that settle with gold
DriftAny sediment left by glaciers: till, outwash, moraine
Driftless AreaSW Wisconsin and nearby, never covered by the last ice
EskerA winding gravel ridge left by a river under the ice
FloatLoose rock or metal moved away from its source (float copper, float boulders)
Flour goldGold so fine it looks like dust; the usual Midwest find
GreenstoneOld altered volcanic rock, the host of most lode gold
LodeGold still in bedrock (veins, shear zones)
Massive sulfide (VMS)A metal-rich sulfide body formed on an ancient sea floor; can carry gold
MoraineA ridge of till at a glacier's edge
OutwashSand and gravel washed out from melting ice; good panning ground
PathfinderAn element like arsenic that travels with gold and is easier to detect
PlacerGold freed from rock and concentrated by water
TillUnsorted glacial debris, from clay to boulders
Up-iceThe direction the glacier came from; where to look for the source

More terms

TermMeaning
ArsenopyriteAn arsenic-iron sulfide that often travels with gold
Calaverite, tellurideGold combined with tellurium; found in a Wausau pegmatite and at Reef
ClassifyScreen material to one size (for example minus 30 mesh) before panning
CrevicingScraping and brushing out bedrock cracks for gold
ElectrumA natural gold-silver alloy
ErraticA boulder carried far by ice
False bedrockA clay or hardpan layer that stops gold like bedrock does
Fire assayThe reliable lab test for gold; old spectrographic gold values are not trusted
g/t, oz/ton, ppb, ppmGrams per tonne; troy ounces per short ton (1 oz/ton is about 34 g/t); parts per billion and per million (1,000 ppb = 1 ppm = 1 g/t)
GossanRusty, weathered cap over a sulfide body
Half-breedNative copper and silver fused in one piece
KettleA hollow left where buried ice melted
Orogenic goldGold in quartz veins along faults and shear zones, formed during mountain building; the style at Reef and behind most world gold
PaleoplacerAn ancient placer turned to rock, like a basal conglomerate
Poor rockMine waste rock in piles; where copper country collectors pick
PyrrhotiteA magnetic iron sulfide common in Reef ore
Shear zoneA band of crushed, stretched rock along a fault; a gold trap
SutureWhere two old crustal blocks collided, like the Niagara suture in Florence County
Tunnel channelA valley cut by water flowing under the ice
VLF-EMVery-low-frequency electromagnetic survey that finds conductors like sulfide lenses
VMSVolcanogenic massive sulfide: a copper-zinc body formed on an ancient sea floor, sometimes gold-rich (Flambeau, Bend, Crandon)

From the old books

What the county histories, travel guides and treasure books say, place by place. Most places here are pins on the map.

Stories pulled from 1850s to 1920s county histories, state historical collections and early geological surveys, all free on archive.org. Every one is also a spot in the Atlas, tagged "From the old books". Always get permission and check land rules before you dig.

How to work an old-book site

  1. Find the old buildings on an 1870s to 1900s county plat map and on 1938 to 1940 aerial photos.

  2. Ask the landowner for written permission. Never dig on public historic sites or in archaeological features.

  3. Search cellar holes, wells and the paths to the river or road. That is where coins and buttons collect.

Books used
BookSpots
Upham, Minnesota Geographic Names (MN Hist. Soc. Collections vol. XVII, 1920)12
Collections of the State Historical Society of Wisconsin, vol. X (1888)10
Randall, History of the Chippewa Valley (1875)8
History of Northern Wisconsin (Western Historical Co., 1881)7
Sawyer, A History of the Northern Peninsula of Michigan, vol. I (1911)7
Geology of Wisconsin, Survey of 1873-1879, vol. I (1883)2
Collections of the State Historical Society of Wisconsin, vol. II (1856)1
Minnesota Geological and Natural History Survey, 23rd Annual Report (1895)1
History of the Upper Peninsula of Michigan (1883)1
Arlyn Colby, The Chippewa Valley Line: The History of the Chippewa Valley & Superior Railway (Milwaukee Road in Eau Claire: bridge M-188, the Half Moon Lake diamond, 1952 aerial)3 (atlas leads)
Gold, silver and copper reports

Kewaunee gold rush of 1836

Wisconsin, Kewaunee County. Mouth of the Kewaunee River

Someone picked up something shiny near the mouth of the Kewaunee River in the early 1830s, and by 1836 rumors of rich gold had John Jacob Astor, Gov. Doty and Salmon P. Chase buying land. A city was platted with 250 lots to rival Chicago. ‘But the gold didn’t pan out.’ State Geologist Chamberlin later ruled the county's rocks out for gold (History of Northern Wisconsin, 1881).

In the field: Almost certainly pyrite or mica. Still, the Lake Michigan beaches and the river mouth are fine coin-and-relic ground, and the 1836 rush makes a great story at the harbor.

Mukwonago drift copper (Cate farm)

Wisconsin, Waukesha County. Mukwonago area (farm not located)

A piece of ‘drift copper, found on the farm of Wallace Cate, of Mukwanago’ was given to the State Historical Society (WHS Collections vol. X). The Green Bay and Lake Michigan ice lobes carried Keweenaw copper hundreds of miles south.

In the field: Float copper sits in glacial till and outwash, not in veins. In plowed fields and gravel pits a detector will find it long before your eye does. One piece does not mean there is another nearby, but drift fields keep giving them up.

Edgerton float copper

Wisconsin, Rock County. Edgerton area

‘Two specimens of float copper, found near Edgerton, Wis.’ were given to the Historical Society (WHS Collections vol. X). Chamberlin (1883) wrote that ‘hundreds, if not thousands’ of such pieces had been picked up in the state, especially in the east and north.

In the field: Ask farmers about ‘heavy green rocks’: many float coppers sit forgotten on porches and fence posts. Work the moraines and outwash with a big coil.

Silver nuggets from the Flambeau headwaters lakes

Wisconsin, Iron / Vilas County. Flambeau headwaters lakes (area only)

‘Small nuggets of silver and specimens of silver ore have occasionally been brought down the river by Indian and half-breed hunters, ever since the first white settlers came here, said to have been gathered on the rocky shores of some of the small lakes, on the head waters of the Flambeau, but nothing could induce those hunters to disclose the precise locality’ (Randall 1875). The Flambeau mine at Ladysmith, on the same river, later produced 334,000 oz of gold and about 3.3 million oz of silver.

In the field: Area pin only. Much of the headwaters is Lac du Flambeau Reservation land, which is closed to outsiders for prospecting and detecting. Downstream public gravel bars along the Flambeau are the legal place to test the story with a pan.

Brunson’s 1843 silver: the La Pointe to Flambeau trail

Wisconsin, Ashland / Iron County. La Pointe–Flambeau trail across the Penokee divide (area only)

Rev. Alfred Brunson, Indian agent at La Pointe in 1843, was given ‘a piece of pure silver … about the value of half a dollar.’ The man ‘picked it out of a rock on or near the divide’ and would not say where. Brunson guessed it lay ‘on or near the trail leading from that lake [Flambeau] to La Pointe’ (letter in Randall 1875).

In the field: The trail crossed the Penokee-Gogebic divide. Keweenawan rocks along that divide do carry native copper with silver specks, so the story is geologically possible. Look for green-stained float in creeks that cross the range, on public forest land.

1870s gold reports at the head springs of the Chippewa

Wisconsin, Ashland / Sawyer County. Headwaters of the Chippewa (area only)

Writing to Randall around 1874, Alfred Brunson mentioned ‘the recent accounts of the discovery of gold in the woods somewhere at or near the head springs of the Chippewa.’ In 1871 William Hassard, prospecting the Penokee Range, ‘found gold and silver ore that assayed $140 to the ton’ (Randall 1875; History of Northern Wisconsin, 1881).

In the field: Area pin. These reports fit the greenstone and quartz-vein rocks north of the East Fork Chippewa. Pan the creeks that drain the Penokee range southward first.

Sacramento: the deserted gold-washing village on the Zumbro (1855)

Minnesota, Dodge County. West edge of Mantorville township, on the Zumbro

‘Sacramento was a village platted in the fall of 1855, on the Zumbro river in the west edge of Mantorville.’ It lost the county seat vote in 1857 and its buildings were moved away. ‘The name, from California, had reference to scanty occurrence of placer gold in the drift of some localities on branches of the Zumbro and Root rivers … One of the places of ill repaid gold washing by the early settlers was near the site’ (Upham 1920).

In the field: Two targets in one spot: a short-lived 1850s village for coins, and drift gravels that settlers actually panned. Pan the inside bends of the Zumbro below Mantorville with permission, and compare with the Oronoco diggings downstream.

Otter Creek ‘gold mine’ (Cunningham & Miner)

Minnesota, Carlton County. Mouth of Otter Creek on the St. Louis River (approximate)

The state survey collected ‘samples of the supposed gold ore, for which mining operations were conducted at the mouth of Otter creek by Cunningham and Miner a few years since. The rock is a compact sericitic schist and the yellow ore is pyrite’ (Minnesota Geological Survey annual report).

In the field: Fool's gold, but the slate and schist belt along the St. Louis River does host real quartz veins elsewhere. Good practice ground for telling pyrite from gold in the pan.

Native copper in the drift above the Cyclops mine, Norway

Michigan, Dickinson County. Cyclops mine, Norway

‘Native copper, evidently brought by glacial action from the Keweenawan measures to the north, has been found in drift above the iron ore body of the Cyclops mine, at Norway’ (Sawyer 1911).

In the field: This shows float copper reaching the Menominee Range. Old mine land may be posted. Work gravel pits and plowed outwash south of the range with permission.

Perkins native copper report

Michigan, Delta County. Perkins

‘Native copper is said to be found in Perkins, Delta county, but the discovery does not seem of commercial importance’ (Sawyer 1911). It is almost certainly glacial float.

In the field: Treat it like any float copper area: a big coil in fields and gravel pits.

Silver Mountain, Baraga County

Michigan, Baraga County. Silver Mountain, near Sidnaw

‘In Baraga county there is an isolated outlier of the Keweenawan formation, known as Silver mountain’ (Sawyer 1911). An 1883 county history adds that ‘an earlier race of miners have left’ traces ‘in several of the gold-bearing streams of the county.’

In the field: Silver Mountain is on Ottawa National Forest land with a summit trail. Pan the creeks draining it for copper and silver specks, and leave any ancient pit untouched.

Lost towns and villages

Dunnville: Lamb’s and McCann’s stopping place (1840s)

Wisconsin, Dunn County. Dunnville, near the Red Cedar–Chippewa confluence

Randall (1875): a man named Lamb ‘stuck his stakes and built the first house in Dunnville, which very soon became a noted stopping place for all the lumbermen and hunters.’ Arthur McCann bought it in 1841 and was shot on his own doorstep after a card game in 1843; Philo Stone then took over the tavern. Dunnville was briefly the Dunn County seat before the town faded.

In the field: Use the steps at the top of this chapter. Much of the low ground is now the Dunnville State Wildlife Area, where you need to check DNR rules before swinging a detector.

Chippewa City: Warren’s farm and fur post (1830s) and the 1857 paper town

Wisconsin, Chippewa County. Chippewa River about 5 miles above Chippewa Falls

Lyman Warren set up the government farm and blacksmith shop ‘at Chippewa City, five miles above the Falls’ in the 1830s and it became ‘quite an important place for the sale of goods, and the collection of furs’ under the American Fur Company. In 1857 speculators platted a second ‘Chippewa City’ near Neil’s Creek, on a rumored railroad crossing. They sold a few lots and opened ‘a saloon or two’ before the Panic of 1857 wiped it out (Randall 1875).

In the field: The pin is approximate (5 miles upriver from Chippewa Falls). The 1830s trading spot is the prize: look for a terrace above the river near a creek mouth on early plats.

Bear Creek townsite above Durand (1855, flooded out)

Wisconsin, Pepin County. Mouth of Bear Creek, 3–4 miles above Durand

Perry Curtis and partners believed the Chippewa bottoms did not flood and in 1855 platted a town ‘near the mouth of Bear Creek, three or four miles above the present village of Durand.’ ‘A hotel, a store or two, and several dwellings were erected,’ but two years of high water left the site ‘under water for several months each year, and the project of building up a town there was forever abandoned’ (Randall 1875).

In the field: A short-lived 1850s hotel and store on river bottoms is a classic spot for seated Liberty coins and trade tokens. Floods since then have buried the ground, so expect targets deeper than usual. Confirm the exact spot on the 1870s plat.

Staffordsville: the vanished village north of Neillsville

Wisconsin, Clark County. Three-quarters of a mile north of Neillsville

L. R. Stafford's village, ‘three-fourths of a mile north of Neillsville,’ had ‘a saw mill, grist mill, hotel, machine shop, etc.’ and ‘was more of a business place than the county seat.’ After he died in 1871 ‘the settlement has entirely disappeared, nothing is left but the hotel,’ which was used as a smallpox pest house and was ‘rapidly falling to pieces’ by 1881 (History of Northern Wisconsin, 1881).

In the field: Use the steps at the top of this chapter.

Neshodana (Gordon): Burnett County’s first village (1855-57)

Wisconsin, Burnett County. Yellow River, 1 mile above the St. Croix (Danbury)

Speculators expecting the St. Croix & Lake Superior Railroad platted Neshodana ‘on the bank of Yellow River, one mile above its confluence with the Saint Croix.’ It had a large sawmill costing $10,000, a store and about a dozen houses. ‘It was a total failure’: the Panic of 1857 ended the railroad. Renamed Gordon, it was named the first county seat in 1856 (History of Northern Wisconsin, 1881).

In the field: Not the modern town of Gordon in Douglas County. The pin is one mile up the Yellow River from Danbury, so check the river terraces on the 1880s plat.

Bay City, Ashland (1856-1860) and its crib dock

Wisconsin, Ashland County. West end of Ashland, Bay City Creek

Bay City was surveyed in 1856 and had ‘a store, hotel and several other buildings’. A crib dock ran about 500 feet into the lake. The town was vacated in 1860 and folded into Ashland as ‘Ellis's division’ (History of Northern Wisconsin, 1881).

In the field: Today this is inside the city of Ashland. The beach and shallow water off the old dock line can be searched after storms. Check city beach and park rules, and get permission on private shoreline.

Newport, Sauk County: the deserted village below the Dells

Wisconsin, Sauk County. Wisconsin River below Wisconsin Dells

An 1881 biography calls it ‘the then flourishing town of Newport, Sauk Co., now a deserted village.’ Newport lost out when the railroad crossed the Wisconsin River at Kilbourn (Wisconsin Dells), and its buildings were moved away (History of Northern Wisconsin, 1881).

In the field: The pin is approximate. Locate the village blocks on the 1859-1870s plats and ask landowners.

City of the Four Lakes and Rowan’s trading post (Pheasant Branch)

Wisconsin, Dane County. Pheasant Branch, head of Lake Mendota

Wallace Rowan's trading post stood ‘just north of the outlet of Pheasant Branch, at the head of Lake Mendota,’ by the 1832 Black Hawk War. Michel St. Cyr held it next. In 1836 the ‘City of the Four Lakes’ was laid out on the same spot, near Livesey's Spring, as a rival for the state capital, and it lost (WHS Collections vol. X).

In the field: Much of this is now Pheasant Branch Conservancy (Middleton), where detecting is not allowed. Use it for the story and check private parcels nearby.

St. Nicholas, Lake Albert Lea (1856-57)

Minnesota, Freeborn County. South side of Lake Albert Lea, Secs. 25–26

‘The first village in this county, platted in the summer of 1856, on the south side of Lake Albert Lea, in sections 25 and 26.’ It lost the 1857 county seat vote, ‘its buildings were removed and the village site became farming land’ (Upham 1920).

In the field: Use the steps at the top of this chapter.

Okaman, Lake Elysian (1857-1867)

Minnesota, Waseca / Le Sueur County. East side of the north end of Lake Elysian

‘Okaman, at the east side of the northern end of Lake Elysian, was an early village, platted March 30, 1857 … Its site was vacated in 1867 and reverted to farm uses’ (Upham 1920).

In the field: Use the steps at the top of this chapter. Lakeshore lots: check shallow water near the old landing too.

Tepeeota: the island town burned in 1859

Minnesota, Wabasha County. Mississippi island, Greenfield township (approximate)

Tepeeota, ‘many houses’ in Dakota, was ‘founded in 1856 on an island of the Mississippi, a former camping ground of Wapashaw’s band.’ After the Panic of 1857, ‘on a March night in 1859, its deserted steam sawmill, three-story hotel, stores, etc., mostly then empty, were burned’ (Upham 1920).

In the field: The pin is approximate (Greenfield township). Most Mississippi islands here are in the Upper Mississippi National Wildlife Refuge, where detecting and digging are prohibited. Check the land status before you go.

Saxton, mouth of Two Island River (1856-58)

Minnesota, Cook County. Mouth of Two Island River

‘At the mouth of this river the village of Saxton was platted by Commodore Saxton, Lyle Hutchins, and others, in August, 1856, but was abandoned two years later’ (Upham 1920).

In the field: This is in the Taconite Harbor area. Shoreline cobble beaches here are agate ground anyway, so check access and look for 1850s cabin sites back from the beach.

Buchanan land-office town (1856-59)

Minnesota, St. Louis County. Lake Superior shore SW of the Knife River mouth

Buchanan was platted in October 1856 ‘on the shore of Lake Superior southwestward from the mouth of Knife river.’ It held the U.S. land office from 1857 to May 1859, then ‘like many other paper towns on the north shore, it never amounted to anything’ (Upham 1920).

In the field: A land office meant cash moving through: every claim was paid at the counter. Find the plat on an 1850s map and ask landowners along the shore.

Dayton (Waseata) on the Red River, abandoned 1862

Minnesota, Otter Tail County. Red River, 4 miles SW of Fergus Falls

Dayton ‘was a village founded before 1860 with the building of a sawmill on the Red river, about four miles southwest from the site of Fergus Falls, and its post office was named Waseata.’ It was ‘permanently abandoned in August, 1862’ (Upham 1920).

In the field: Use the steps at the top of this chapter.

Vicksburg, Renville County (1867-1878)

Minnesota, Renville County. Sec. 19, Flora township

‘Vicksburg, a former village in section 19, Flora, platted in 1867, was superseded in 1878 by the railway village of Sacred Heart, to which its buildings were removed’ (Upham 1920).

In the field: Use the steps at the top of this chapter.

Itasca townsite and trading post, Anoka County (1852)

Minnesota, Anoka County. Secs. 19 and 30, Ramsey township

Itasca was ‘a townsite platted in 1852 on sections 19 and 30 in this township, near an Indian trading post,’ with the first post office in Anoka County. ‘Both the village and the railway station have been abandoned’ (Upham 1920).

In the field: Use the steps at the top of this chapter.

Flat Rock: Delta County’s first settlement (1830)

Michigan, Delta County. Flat Rock, near Gladstone

‘The first settler of Delta county seems to have been Louis A. Roberts, a trader who located at Flat Rock in 1830.’ Two unnamed men built ‘a small sawmill, the first in that section,’ which the Smith brothers abandoned in 1844 (Sawyer 1911).

In the field: Use the steps at the top of this chapter.

Forts, trading posts and old sites

Porterville and the Blue Mill: the 1847 flood

Wisconsin, Eau Claire County. East side of early Eau Claire (approximate)

In June 1847 the Chippewa rose twelve feet overnight. The new double sawmill on the Eau Claire River was ‘borne almost bodily away’, and ‘some of the heaviest timbers, and heavily ironed wheels belonging to the mill … lodged high upon the slope of the hill back of Porterville.’ That same day David Dale Owen’s federal geological survey party was camped at Randall’s Blue Mill (built 1842-43, taken down 1864) (Randall 1875).

In the field: The pin is approximate, on the east side of early Eau Claire. Use the 1878 bird's-eye view of Eau Claire and early plats to place Porterville and the Blue Mill. A flood that throws mill wheels up a hillside also scatters everything lighter, so old terraces above the river are worth a slow, careful look with permission.

Helena on the Wisconsin River: ‘entirely deserted’ in 1833

Wisconsin, Iowa County. Wisconsin River near Tower Hill

A soldier in the 1833 dragoon march wrote that Helena ‘consisted of ten or fifteen houses; but was entirely deserted, except two men.’ The town revived around the shot tower and faded again when the railroad passed it by (WHS Collections vol. X).

In the field: The shot tower is in Tower Hill State Park, where you may not detect without a permit. The old town ground near the river is mostly private: ask first.

Fort Defiance stockade (1832)

Wisconsin, Lafayette County. Sec. 20, T4N R3E, SE of Mineral Point

‘Fort Defiance, a stockade post situated on section twenty, in Town four North, Range three East, commanded by Capt. Robert C. Hoard.’ On June 14, 1832 a hatless rider galloped in with news that set off the Battle of the Pecatonica (WHS Collections vol. II).

In the field: Sec. 20, T4N R3E is about five miles southeast of Mineral Point. The pin is approximate, so locate the section on a plat and check the state historical marker for the exact field.

Fort Hamilton and Hamilton’s Diggings (Wiota)

Wisconsin, Lafayette County. Wiota

‘Fort Hamilton (now Wiota), where there was a block-house and a small settlement of miners. Considerable mining had been done at that place’ (WHS Collections vol. X). Alexander Hamilton's son William ran the diggings here.

In the field: Old lead diggings show up as aspen clumps and pocked ground (see the ‘Masonic weed’ tip in the Field Book).

Gratiot’s Grove stockade and smelting furnaces (1832)

Wisconsin, Lafayette County. Southeast of Shullsburg

In 1832 families fled from the surrounding diggings to Gratiot's Grove, where ‘a strong stockade was being built around the store and warehouse.’ Henry Gratiot stayed in command. The next spring the block-house and stockade were ‘converted into cord-wood’ (Mrs. Adele Gratiot's narrative, WHS Collections vol. X).

In the field: Southeast of Shullsburg. Furnace sites leave slag and lead drips; the store and stockade ground is where coins were lost.

Blue Mounds blockhouse (1832)

Wisconsin, Dane County. East of Blue Mounds village

‘Blue Mounds, where we found a block house. There had been a settlement here, but the people had all left on account of the Indians, who had killed some of the settlers’ (WHS Collections vol. X).

In the field: The fort site is marked. Blue Mound State Park, on the mound itself, does not allow detecting. Ask private landowners along the old military road.

Oliver Armel’s trading house, Madison: 1798 cent and Spanish silver

Wisconsin, Dane County. Near Johnson Street, Madison

Madison's first building was the French trader Oliver Armel's trading house near today's Johnson Street. Two deserters from Fort Winnebago were arrested there in 1832. ‘An American cent of 1798, and several Spanish silver coins, picked up in 1880 in Sorenson’s garden, may have been lost by the intoxicated soldiers, and possibly mark the very spot’ (WHS Collections vol. X).

In the field: Urban land now; this is a story pin. The lesson for the field: a trader's site leaves Spanish reales and large cents, so treat any 1830s trading spot the same way.

Old French fort, Lower Town, Prairie du Chien

Wisconsin, Crawford County. Lower Town, Prairie du Chien (farm lot 39)

In 1885 old settlers placed ‘the old French fort’ near the Mississippi ‘on the west end of farm lot No. 39, in what is now called Lower Town.’ Congressman O. B. Thomas called it ‘this historic old treasure trove.’ S. A. Clark dug up burned limestone from three fireplaces, and the east rampart line was still visible (WHS Collections vol. X).

In the field: Lower Town is near the old Pig's Eye slough, south of the court house. Much of Prairie du Chien's old ground is a protected historic district.

Old Wadena trading post and ferry (Crow Wing River)

Minnesota, Wadena County. Crow Wing River crossing, Thomastown township

The Wadena trading post and ferry stood ‘on the west bluff of the Crow Wing river’ between the mouths of the Leaf and Partridge rivers. In its busiest years, 1855-1860, ‘more than a hundred people lived at this trading post,’ but by 1899 ‘only their cellar holes remained to mark the spot’ (Upham 1920).

In the field: Old Wadena is now a county historic site, so treat it as look only. The ox-cart trail approaches and ford banks outside the site, on private land with permission, are where travelers lost coins and harness brass.

Georgetown Hudson’s Bay Company post (1859)

Minnesota, Clay County. Red River at Georgetown

‘Georgetown was established as a trading post of the Hudson Bay Company in 1859; was abandoned in September, 1862, during the Sioux outbreak; and was reestablished in 1864’ (Upham 1920).

In the field: HBC tokens and trade goods are possible near Red River posts. The riverbank is mostly private, so ask first.

Sandy Point, Lake Pepin: French stockades and the cannon-ball ‘cache’

Minnesota, Goodhue County. Sandy Point (Point au Sable), Lake Pepin

Pike (1806) wrote that the French ‘built a stockade on Lake Pepin on the west shore just below Point du Sable.’ The post was rebuilt in 1732 with pickets enclosing 120 feet square and four bastions. ‘The cannon balls found in the ground at Frontenac station may have been discharged in some engagement … or they may have been taken from the fort, after its abandonment, and placed in a cache’ (WHS Collections vol. X).

In the field: Much of the point is in Frontenac State Park, where detecting needs a permit and digging is not allowed. Use it for the story; private farmland back from the lake is ask-first.

Chappee’s stockade post at the Menominee mouth (1805) and Farnsworth’s mill (1832)

Michigan, Marinette / Menominee County. Menominee River mouth, Marinette side

Louis Chappee built ‘the first permanent trading post on the river’ around 1805, ‘almost after a fashion of a fort, with heavy palisades.’ In 1822 William Farnsworth of the American Fur Company threw his goods out while he was away and took it over. Farnsworth and Brush built the first sawmill on the Menominee nearby in 1832; ‘the dam was washed out and the mill was abandoned’ (Sawyer 1911).

In the field: The pin is approximate (Marinette side, near the river mouth). City land now; this is a story pin.

Chappee Rapids: Chappee’s second post (1822-1852)

Michigan, Menominee County. Foot of Chappee Rapids, Menominee River

Thrown out of his first post, Chappee ‘loaded his provisions, belongings and helpers into batteaux and made his way up river, landing at the foot of the rapids that have since borne his name,’ where he built another trading post. He traded there until he died in 1852 (Sawyer 1911).

In the field: Thirty years of trading on one spot can leave trade silver, buttons, gun parts and coins. The pin is approximate, so find the rapids' foot on old maps and ask the landowners.

Jackson Forge on the Carp River (1847-1857)

Michigan, Marquette County. Carp River, 3 miles east of Negaunee

‘In 1847 the Jackson Mining Company built the old forge on the Carp river, three miles east of Negaunee, which, like all other forges in the early days of Marquette county, steadily lost money … until it was finally abandoned in 1857’ (Sawyer 1911).

In the field: The forge site is a marked historic site; treat it as look only. Forge workers' cabins and the road to Marquette were in the woods around it, so check land status before detecting anywhere nearby.

Look only

Rice Lake pipestone quarry (sacred site)

Wisconsin, Barron County. W½ Sec. 27, T35N R10W, near Rice Lake

Randall (1875) placed the ‘Red Pipe-stone mountain’ on ‘the west half of section twenty-seven, town thirty-five north, of range ten west.’ An Ojibwe guide led the 1843 Brunson party there in secret and left tobacco ‘to appease the Manitou … on account of the trespass on the sacred spot.’

In the field: Look only. This is a sacred quarry on private land. Do not collect, dig or detect here.

Crow Wing village (fur trade center)

Minnesota, Crow Wing County. Crow Wing State Park

Crow Wing was ‘the center of Indian trading for all the upper country’ from about 1837 and had about 600 people in 1866. Like Old Wadena, its buildings disappeared and only cellar holes remained (Upham 1920).

In the field: Inside Crow Wing State Park: no metal detecting without a permit, and no digging. Visit for the story and the layout of a trail town.

From Ghost Towns of Wisconsin (Stark, 1977)

William F. Stark visited and photographed 16 Wisconsin ghost towns. These notes cover chapters 1 to 5, read from your borrowed archive.org copy. All five sites are on private land, so ask before you set foot on any of them. Each one is a pin on the Atlas.

Sinipee, Grant County (1836-1839)

In 1836 lead miners tired of Galena's prices formed the Sinipee Company with Payton Vaughn and platted their own Mississippi port. They built a two-story Stone House hotel with a ballroom, and Zachary Taylor and Jefferson Davis stayed there. In 1839 a flood left stagnant pools behind, and malaria emptied the town.

Finding it: go to the Fenley farm under a big sandstone bluff, about 3 miles north of the Dubuque bridge. A quarter mile on, a faint road through the woods follows the old main street. The Stone House foundation sits against the bluff on the east side of the road, beside a spring that runs out of the rock. The pioneer cemetery is on Sinipee Heights, 400 ft up a steep ravine; leave it alone.

Port Ulao, Ozaukee County (1847-1860s)

James Gifford built a 1,000-ft pier and a wooden chute down a 200-ft bluff. Farmers' cordwood went down the chute to fuel Great Lakes steamers. His plank road west, surfaced with charcoal and burned clay, is now County Q. Charles Guiteau, who later shot President Garfield, spent five years of his boyhood here. In 1862 troops came ashore at the pier to put down the Ozaukee draft riot.

Finding it: take County Q (Ulao Road) east from Hwy 43. The Guiteau brick house is about 1 mile east. A quarter mile past it, the bluff begins, and lines of apple trees and lilacs mark the old wagon road down to the beach. On the beach where the pier stood, look for cribbing, spikes and coins from the steamer era. Check who owns the access first.

Oil City, Monroe County (1842-1902)

In 1866 a con man named Tichnor 'discovered' oil by a spring on the upper Kickapoo River and sold stock in the Gem Petroleum Company. The well he sank struck pure artesian water instead. Locals then found the buried barrel his oil had come from. Despite that, the village grew a gristmill, a sawmill and a cooper shop, until the railroad passed it by.

Finding it: go about 4 miles south of Wilton, at the mouth of Moore's Creek. A weathered wooden 'derrick' still stands over the bubbling spring. This is Driftless country, so expect no glacial gold. The mill sites are the spots to search.

Gratiot's Grove, Lafayette County (1825-1840s)

By 1827 the grove had nine lead smelters and about 1,000 people. In 1828 it was called 'the most important place between Chicago and Galena.' Henry Gratiot's 1835 limestone house still stands. Lead was still being mined under the site in the 1970s, and you could see the mine air vents at the surface. About a mile south, Fortunatus Berry's 1829 stagecoach tavern lost many people to cholera in the 1850s; a DAR marker stands 2 miles south of Shullsburg.

Finding it: drive about a mile south of Shullsburg on County U. Lafayette County also has these lead-camp ghost towns: Aetna, Natchez, Cork Hollow, Buncome and White Oak Springs.

Old Lead Road: from 1828 until the railroads came in the late 1850s, ox teams hauled lead from Galena through Mineral Point to Milwaukee. A stone marker 2 miles south of New Glarus stands on a stretch of the road that is known for certain. The site of Exeter, a lead camp, lies just east of New Glarus. Hamilton's Diggings is now Wiota.

Pleasant Ridge, Grant County (1848-1961)

This was a farming settlement of freed slaves and their descendants, with about 200 people by 1900. District School No. 5 taught Black and white children together and may have been the first integrated school in America.

Finding it: from Lancaster, go 5 miles west on Hwy 81. Opposite the old 'Shurman's Cheese Factory' sign, turn right onto the gravel road. At the T, turn left and go half a mile to the hilltop cemetery. A second cemetery from 1883, with 11 graves, lies across the valley. Visit only. No detecting here.

Voree, Walworth County (1844-1856)

James Strang's Mormon city. He claimed to have dug up prophetic metal plates on the 'Hill of Promise'. In 1849 most of his followers left for Beaver Island, where he was crowned King James in 1850. After he was shot in 1856, he was brought back to Voree and died here.

Strang held 105 acres on the White River. He said the plates lay about 2 ft down, at the foot of an oak near the crest of the oak-covered hill above the village.

Finding it: Hwy 11 crosses the White River about 2 miles west of Burlington. Just west of the bridge, on the north side, is the sandstone house where the Voree Herald was printed. It is a private home. A stone marker with a metal map stands on the riverbank across the road. The Hill of Promise and the quarry are just east of the river, south of the road. Strang's grave is in Burlington Cemetery. The area is now called Spring Prairie.

Old Belmont, Lafayette County (1836)

This was Wisconsin's first territorial capitol. The legislature met here for 46 days in 1836, with the members sleeping on the floor. The town faded after the railroad went through 3 miles to the south.

Finding it: First Capitol state historic site, about 10 miles southwest of Mineral Point. Two buildings are restored on 2 acres. No detecting on the site.

Rock Island, Door County (1830s-1860s)

From the mid-1830s, a fishing village of about 100 people lived in the southeast cove. The 1836 Pottawatomie Light on the north bluff was Wisconsin's first lighthouse.

The fishing village, called the 'Illinois Colony', peaked in the late 1840s and 1850s. The last fisherman left in 1890.

Treasure story: James McNeil owned most of the south shore and bragged about his hidden 'yellow boys', meaning gold coins. He was found shot beside his chicken coop. His killer was never caught, and no one has reported finding the coins.

Finding it: take the ferry from Washington Island. Lilacs still mark the house pits in the southeast cove. The whole island is a state park, so you may look but not detect or dig.

Getting to Rock Island: take the Gills Rock ferry to Washington Island, drive about 8 miles to Jackson Harbor, then ride the Karfi passenger boat (about 10 minutes, hourly, June 1 to October 15). The village foundations are in the east-shore cove near Thordarson's stone water tower. John Boon (died 1866) is buried in one of the two graveyards. A walk around the island takes about 3 hours.

Helena, Iowa County (1828-1861)

Helena was a lead port across the Wisconsin River from Spring Green. In 1831 Daniel Whitney's men dug a 120-ft shaft straight down through the sandstone bluff, with a 60-ft tower on top and a tunnel out to the river. Molten lead was dropped down it to make rifle shot until about 1861. The lead came from Dodgeville, Ridgeway and Pokerville.

Finding it: Tower Hill State Park. The shot tower and the tunnel can be walked, and the Old Helena Cemetery is in the park. State park: no detecting.

Seeleyburg, Vernon County (1856-1900s)

Dempster Seeley dammed the Kickapoo and was sawing white pine by 1857. The village had a Main Street, a cross road called 'The Lane', a store, a cobbler and an apothecary. It was platted in 1867, and the floods of 1897 and 1905 helped finish it.

Finding it: about 1 mile north of La Farge on old Hwy 131. Two cemeteries sit on the hills at each end of the valley, and a wooden house stands on the highway. Walk about a quarter mile west down a tree-lined lane to reach Seeley's dam. This is Driftless country, so no glacial gold, but the mill and store lots are worth a look with permission.

Newport, Sauk County (1849-1870s)

Newport stood on the Wisconsin River about 1.5 miles below today's Wisconsin Dells. It boomed to about 2,000 people on lumber rafting and held a charter to dam the river. Byron Kilbourn then put his railroad crossing 2 miles upstream, at what is now Wisconsin Dells, and Newport was empty within 20 years.

Finding it: Dawn Manor, an 1855 sandstone mansion on Sauk County Hwy A about 1.5 miles south of Wisconsin Dells, marks the west end of town. On the far bank, cellar hollows, lilacs and locust trees show where the houses stood. It is a good detecting candidate if you get landowner permission.

Hidden beer vault: in 1977 Stark was led through a thickly wooded ravine near the Dells to an almost hidden opening in the rocks. Inside was a cave-like room, the 'beer vault' of the Hoffman Brewery, cut when Newport boomed in the early 1850s. It is on private land, so go only with the owner's permission and a guide.

Dunnville, Dunn County (1840-1900s): closest to Eau Claire

In 1842 a man named Sawyer shot the tavern keeper, Arthur McCann, at his own door after a card game and was never caught. Amos Colburn's hotel stood on the west bank. On the east bank, Knapp, Stout and Co. built a company store with a dance hall upstairs (1854), the Tainter House hotel (1858) and a steamboat warehouse. Paddle-wheelers came up the Red Cedar this far, and a stage ran daily to Menomonie. The last lumber raft left on August 11, 1901.

Finding it: go about 12 miles south of Menomonie on Hwy 25, then east on County Y about 1 mile to the Red Cedar River bridge. The town stood on both banks. The Colburn House still stands on the first high ground on the west bank. The Tainter House, store and warehouse were at the boat landing on the east bank. The 1856 Caddie Woodlawn house is in a 5-acre park on Hwy 25, about a mile from the river. Much of the bottomland is the Dunnville State Wildlife Area, so check DNR rules before you detect. The Red Cedar gravel bars below the old landing are worth a pan.

Dover, Dane/Iowa County (1844-1860s)

Dover was founded by the British Temperance Emigration Society. Liverpool workingmen paid in a shilling a week to buy Wisconsin land. The settlement was called Gorstville until 1846.

Finding it: Hwy 14, about 20 miles west of Madison between Mazomanie and Arena. A state marker stands with a small park and a cemetery where only Culvers are buried. The Appleby homestead and the old hotel are on the south side of Hwy 14. The Mazomanie Historical Society holds Dover artifacts and maps.

Pokerville (West Blue Mounds), Dane/Iowa County (1828-1880s)

In 1828 Ebenezer Brigham struck rich lead here and claimed 1,400 acres. Al Pape's 1975 map in the book marks Brigham's 'special rich lead ore shafts' and diggings southeast near the site of Fort Blue Mounds (1832), the site of Brigham's tavern off Military Ridge Road, and the old depot.

Finding it: about 1 mile west of Blue Mounds village, on Hwy 18-151. The Marty farmhouse, an 1830s stage inn, is the only building left on the original site. Look for pocked ground and galena. The diggings are on private land.

La Rue, Sauk County (1898-1960)

La Rue was an iron boomtown of more than 500 people. The Sauk, Iroquois and Illinois mines ran from 1898 to 1906. The Rattlesnake quartzite quarry, a mile south, worked until 1957.

Finding it: about 2 miles southwest of North Freedom. The Mid-Continent Railway steam train passes the La Rue crossing (Klingenmeyer's Bar) on its way to the quarry. Mine dumps are good for hematite specimens. Stay out of the shafts.

Turtleville, Rock County (1840s-1876)

William Hodson's flour mill, distillery and 17-room mansion stood here. In the Civil War he shipped unstamped whiskey hidden under potatoes, and he lost everything to the government by 1872.

Finding it: Shopiere Road at Lathers Road, about 8 miles northeast of Beloit. The mansion foundation and its arched whiskey vaults are still visible. Cross the 1887 iron truss bridge over Turtle Creek, go a few hundred yards, and turn left on Creek Road. The cemetery entrance is on the left.

Primary sources Stark cites, worth looking up: Wisconsin Historical Collections vols. I, X, XV and XIX; Strong, Territory of Wisconsin (1885); History of Monroe County (1892); Gregory, Southeastern Wisconsin (1932); the Belmont Gazette and Wisconsin Democrat (1836); and the Grant County Historical Society's Greene Papers on Pleasant Ridge.

From Discovering Wisconsin (Brody, 1973)

A 1973 travel guide built around roadside historical markers. Most of it is tourism, but the markers point straight at old roads, camps and boom towns. About 65 spots are now on the Atlas (search "Brody"). Many are geology, which goes on a new layer called Rocks, caves and landmarks.

Best detecting leads (permission first):

  • Old Military Roads. The 1835-38 road runs along Military Ridge (US 18/151) through the lead region; Brigham's inn at Blue Mounds was a stop. The 1863 road runs from Green Bay to Copper Harbor (roughly Hwy 55); its 1880s way stations were Otter Slide, the Gauthier Place and Mag Lawe's. The Keshena stretch is Menominee land.

  • Plank roads. The Sheboygan-Fond du Lac road through Greenbush (Wade House) and the 58-mile Watertown Plank Road from Milwaukee: look at tollgates, taverns and teamster stops.

  • Stage stops and crossroads. Wilmot (1848), Milton House where three trails met, Hawks Inn at Delafield, and Henry Janes' ferry at Janesville.

  • Payment and gathering grounds. The Poygan Paygrounds west of Winneconne, where the Menominee were paid every October; Friol Island trading ground at Prairie du Chien; the Delavan circus winter quarters (26 circuses, 1847-94); Waukesha's 34 spa hotels.

  • Boom and bust towns. Hurley's Silver Street, where drunk miners were "rolled"; Phillips before the 1894 fire; Black River Falls; Prescott's raftsmen; the Gogebic boom camps (54 mines by 1886, crash in 1887).

  • Lead-region dumps. The marker 1 mi west of Shullsburg says the old mining centers are ghost towns with only refuse dumps and pockmarked land. Good for galena, sphalerite and old tools.

  • Ghost towns. Morse and Shenagolden (lumber, Ashland County), plus Dover, Helena and Newport, which were already on the map from Stark.

Look only, never dig: Aztalan, the Old Copper Culture Cemetery at Oconto (about 7,500 years old), Butte des Morts, Man Mound, Lizard Mounds, the Wyalusing, Plum City, Beloit, Cutter Park and Sheboygan mounds, Vita Spring at Beaver Dam, Gullickson's Glen and Roche-a-Cri rock art, the Bad Axe and Brule (1842) battlefields, the French cemeteries near Radisson and Prairie du Chien, and Squaw Island in Lake Duroy.

Fun lore: Joe Saltis's summer hideout at Winter, the Lost Dauphin at De Pere, the Sparta "Gem Petroleum" oil hoax, Kewaunee's fake gold strike, the hermit of Holy Hill, and the steamer Phoenix, which burned off Sheboygan in 1847 with Dutch immigrants carrying their savings.

Still missing from the book: pp 1-7, 40-45 and 164-169, plus pp 303-357, which are campsite lists.

From the old travel booklets (1889 and 1921)

Wisconsin Central, Summer of 1889. This is the railroad's resort guide. Big resort hotels and their docks and picnic groves dropped coins for decades. The best Wisconsin leads:

  • The Hotel Chequamegon at Ashland held 500 guests, and steamers ran from its dock to Washburn, Bayfield and the Apostles.

  • The Cedar Lake Park Hotel was near Slinger.

  • The Island Park Hotel stood on a Lake Winnebago island five miles from Oshkosh, and Roberts' Resort was on Doty Island in Neenah.

  • Kellogg's Medicinal Spring was at Mukwonago.

  • Lake De Neveu, outside Fond du Lac, had a colony of cottages and tents.

  • Waukesha had more than 30 hotels, and the Fountain Spring House alone held 800 guests.

  • Phillips had four hotels in 1889, the State Park Hotel, Lake View House, National Hotel and Northwestern House, which all burned in the 1894 fire.

Milwaukee Journal, The Call of the Open Road (1921). This is an early motor-touring guide. Its best lead is the list of more than 40 official auto tourist camps from 1921, often in town parks or old fairgrounds. Families camped there all summer and lost coins, keys and tokens. Near Eau Claire:

  • The city camp was 1.25 miles from downtown.

  • A favorite camp stood on Hwy 12 at Elk Creek, about 8 miles west.

  • Chippewa Falls camped tourists in Irving Park.

Others:

  • Amherst (the old fairgrounds) and Weyauwega (the fairgrounds)

  • De Pere (by the river) and Superior (on the Nemadji River)

  • Wausau (Rothschild Park)

  • Crandon (Rat Lake, and Lake Hilbert toward Florence)

  • Abbotsford, Clintonville, Brillion, Chilton, Downing, Tomah, Sparta and Viroqua

The guide also points to the Ableman Narrows gorge, Rib Hill, the Mayville dolomite bluffs, Monument Rock south of Viroqua, and the St. Nazianz colony of 1854. Its list of effigy mounds is a reminder of where not to dig: Green Lake's Sugar Loaf, Myrick Park in La Crosse, the Madison and Menasha effigies, and Lake Park in Milwaukee.

Full read of the three big books (Oct. 2026): 319 new spots, 177 cards enriched

The three biggest books in the project files were read page by page in October 2026: Sawyer's History of the Northern Peninsula of Michigan (671 pages), Upham's Minnesota Geographic Names (767 pages, every county with its vanished villages, post offices, mills, ferries and trading posts) and the 1856 Wisconsin Historical Collections vol. II (621 pages: Lockwood, Shaw, Baird, Parkison and Brunson on Green Bay, Prairie du Chien, the lead rush and the Black Hawk War). Every place named was checked against the pins already on the map: 177 matched an existing card and the book's words were added to it; the rest became new pins, placed from the book's own directions, GNIS, Wikipedia township and village pages and the old topographic sheets. Confidence A is on the spot, B within a section, C a township or landmark estimate (about a mile): read the pin evidence on each card.

Leads the books locate only by description (not pinned; the words to take to the plat map or old topo):

  • First school on the Menominee Range: logging camp between Vulcan and the mouth of the Sturgeon (Dickinson, MI): in a logging camp, between the Vulcan and the mouth of the Sturgeon (Sawyer 1911 p. 539) logging camp between Vulcan and the mouth of the Sturgeon River (Menominee River), c.1877; no closer clue in Sawyer
  • McLeod's wooden mill at Twin Island Rapids (1841) (Menominee, MI): eighteen miles up river at Twin Island Rapids (Sawyer 1911 p. 561) Twin Island Rapids on the Menominee River ~18 river miles above the mouth (Koss/Grand Rapids reach); McLeod's 1841 wooden mill
  • Edgemere stamp mill (Adventure Consolidated), Lake Superior shore (Ontonagon, MI): the stamp mill at Edgemere, Lake Superior (Sawyer 1911 p. 502) Edgemere stamp mill site on the Lake Superior shore of Ontonagon County, terminus of the Adventure Consolidated's mill railroad (1902); check 1900s Ontonagon County plat for 'Edgemere'
  • Old Mapleton village (1856) (Blue Earth, MN): the older village which had been platted in June, 1856 (superseded by railway village of Mapleton, 1871) (Upham 1920 p. 62) Plat: 1856 Mapleton village plat, Mapleton Twp, relative to the 1871 railway town
  • Minnewashta, Pleasant View and Vinland summer-home colonies (Carver, MN): Minnewashta, NE end of Lake Minnewashta; Pleasant View, section 1, Chanhassen, north end of Long lake; Vinland, section 2, Chanhassen, south end of Christmas lake (Upham 1920 p. 83) Plat: NE end of Lake Minnewashta; N end Long Lake sec 1 Chanhassen; S end Christmas Lake sec 2 Chanhassen
  • Old Lakeville village (superseded 1869) (Dakota, MN): When the Hastings and Dakota railroad was built there, in 1869, a new village site was chosen ... This village superseded the older Lakeville (Upham 1920 p. 167) Plat: original Lakeville plat 1855 on the St. Paul-St. Peter military road at Prairie (Marion) Lake
  • Buchanan village and sawmill, North Middle Zumbro (Dodge, MN): formerly a small village having a sawmill, on the North Middle branch of the Zumbro river (Upham 1920 p. 172) Plat: Buchanan village and sawmill on North Middle Branch Zumbro River, Dodge Co.
  • Camp Creek immigrant camping place (Fillmore, MN): Camp creeks ... the last having been a favorite camping place for immigrants (Upham 1920 p. 196) Plat: immigrant camping place on Camp Creek, Fillmore Co. (Upham: 'the last' of the Camp creeks)
  • Point Wakon painted scalp-dance stone, Breezy Point (Hennepin, MN): an extremely narrow headland half a mile in length, running out from the southern shore, since named Breezy point (Upham 1920 p. 233) Find Breezy Point (Point Wakon) half-mile headland on the 1870s Minnetonka plat; painted boulder on the point
  • Pomroy and Bergman logging camps (Kanabec, MN): John Pomroy, a pioneer lumberman who had a logging camp beside the lake ...   • Rush Lake logging station (St. Louis, MN): Duluth and Northeastern railroad, beside Rush lake (Upham 1920 p. 489) Look for Rush Lake station on the D&NE line between Saginaw and Hornby on a 1910s railway map
  • Stroud logging station (St. Louis, MN): Duluth and Northeastern railway, six miles southwest of Rush Lake (Upham 1920 p. 490) Locate Rush Lake station first, then 6 mi SW along the D&NE grade
  • Col. James Morrison's farm: Dodge's council with White Crow's Winnebagoes (June 1832) (Iowa, WI): 'marched the whole body off to Col. JAMES MORRISON'S farm, where he held a council with them in the presence of Col. GRATIOT'; 'From MORRISON'S place, Col. DODGE proceeded to Gratiot's Grove, halting a while at Fort Defiance' (WHS Coll. II, 1856 p. 339) Col. James Morrison's farm (Iowa County, 1832), likely the Morrison place south of Blue Mounds toward Mineral Point; check 1830s surveys
  • Bullen's Bridge, Salem (Kenosha, WI): located in the town of Salem, at the place still known as Bullen's Bridge (WHS Coll. II, 1856 p. 469) Bullen's Bridge over the Fox River in the Town of Salem (Kenosha Co.); find on 1860s plat
  • Knapp's hermitage at the mouth of Knapp Creek (Richland, WI): a trapper named KNAPP, whose secluded hermitage was situated in the vicinity of the mouth of a stream near the south west corner of the county, which stream subsequently received his name (WHS Coll. II, 1856 p. 489) mouth of Knapp Creek into the Wisconsin River, SW corner of Richland County (Town of Eagle/Orion reach); Knapp's 1841 cabin

II, 1856 p. 259) Winnebago principal camp July 1832, east bank ~60 river miles above Prairie du Chien; no closer clue

Wisconsin gold target areas

Research notebook, Oct 2026. Every spot it names is on the map.

·

The best odds for new gold sit along the shear zones and volcanic districts around Wisconsin's known deposits, where thick glacial cover has hidden bedrock from past explorers.

Main map: Wisconsin Gold and Treasure Atlas. All 196 spots from this document are in one layered map: lode targets, placer traps on the gold streams, panning spots, gold reports, old riverbeds, gravel pits, treasure stories and metal detecting sites. It has a "Start here" list of 13 picks, a distance filter from Eau Claire, and Google Maps directions for every spot.

Lake Superior gold: Lake Superior Gold Map. Superior Lobe ice ground up the copper- and gold-bearing rock around western Lake Superior and spread it south as red drift. The older advance (River Falls) reached Hudson, Menomonie and Foster, about 20 miles from Eau Claire. Most of the gold reports near home sit on this red drift: Rock Elm and Plum creeks, the Hudson nugget, River Falls, Knapp, Lucas and Eau Galle. The map shows the drift zones (sketched from published descriptions), the source rock, and the Lake Duluth flood channel down the Brule and St. Croix. It also has 212 spots: panning spots, stream traps, gold finds, source mines, copper prospects, USGS chemistry highs and gravel pits.

New data (Oct 2026): where the evidence now points

Four new data sources were added: the USGS 2025 high-resolution airborne magnetic survey, the USGS geochemical database (about 3,100 soil, stream and glacial till samples in northern Wisconsin), 1-meter USGS LiDAR terrain at 10 sites, and the Wisconsin Geological Survey drill-core inventory and well records. Re-scoring every target with all of them moves Florence County to the top.

What changed

  • Florence County is now the lead. Magnetic highs H8, H6 and H1 each have three or more independent clues. Around H8, glacial till runs up to 79 ppm arsenic (normal is about 4) and 11 ppm antimony, a classic pairing near orogenic gold. H6 and H1 have never been drilled.
  • The data passes a sanity check. The strongest chemistry in the state sits right on the known Bend deposit: drill core with 290 ppb gold and nearly 0.5% copper, surrounded by glacial till at 2-4x normal gold.
  • A Taylor County till-gold belt stands out: about 28 till samples run 20-40 ppb gold (normal about 10), and the area 15-25 km east of Bend has no exploration drilling.
  • LiDAR found 12 dug-looking pits: round, steep holes 13-22 m wide and 1.2-2.9 m deep on otherwise smooth ground, most with a spoil pile beside them. Three are about 1 km from Florence magnetic highs. Plum Creek has four. The buried known deposits (Reef, Bend, Lynne) show none, which is expected.
  • The arsenic-antimony spot north of H8 was already drilled. Minatome cored 14 holes there, and the core is still in the state library, so it can be re-sampled rather than re-drilled.
  • Caution: gold values from the older spectrographic lab method (hundreds of 10-12 ppm readings) are unreliable and were thrown out. Only fire-assay and atomic-absorption gold was used.

Chemistry: where pathfinder metals spike

LiDAR: dug-looking pits at 10 sites

Look-alikes include gravel borrow holes, tree-throw holes, old wells or cellars, and in Pierce County natural sinkholes. A site visit settles it in minutes.

2025 high-resolution magnetics

The 2025 survey covers only Wisconsin north of about 45.7 N. Rock grain near T4 and LaSalle Falls trends WNW (about 107 degrees), not NE like Reef, so the Reef fault model does not carry over to Florence.

Data: USGS 2025 airborne magnetic survey, USGS National Geochemical Database, USGS 3DEP 1 m LiDAR, WGNHS rock core and depth-to-bedrock services.

Second pass: host rock, the Niagara suture and a sinkhole check

  • The Florence targets sit on the Niagara suture. The Macrostrat geologic map (from USGS Open-File Report 97-455) shows the boundary between the Pembine-Wausau volcanic arc (south) and the old continental margin (north) running right through H6 and pit P3, and past H10 and the most arsenic-rich till sample. Big crustal sutures are where orogenic gold usually collects, so this lifts H6 and H1 to the top of the ranking.
  • Host rock now counts. Targets on volcanic rock score higher than those on granite or gneiss. T1 (Wolf River granite), T5 (gneiss) and T6 (granite) drop. T2, T3, T4 and the Taylor till-gold belt rise to Tier B.
  • Two Plum Creek pits are probably sinkholes. LiDAR pits 2 and 9 sit on Prairie du Chien dolomite, which dissolves into natural sinkholes. They no longer count as evidence.
  • North of the suture, iron formation is mapped (Paint River Group). It explains some of the strong magnetic highs, and iron formation can itself host gold in the Lake Superior region, so H8 stays in play.

Takeaway: professional money in 2026 is going into Bend, not Reef, and nobody is publicly working the Florence ground. The very high tellurium at Bend also supports the earlier telluride-gold idea around Wausau.

What the known deposits are worth on paper

Gold was about $4,166 per ounce on Oct 16, 2026. Using the old (not current, not compliant) historical estimates:

  • Reef: 454,000 tons at 0.262-0.308 oz/ton is about 119,000-140,000 oz of gold, or roughly $495-582 million in the ground.
  • Bend: about 311,000 oz of gold in its two zones (plus copper and silver), or roughly $1.3 billion of gold in the ground.
  • These are gross metal values, not profit; mining costs, recovery and permitting decide whether any of it is economic. At today's price, deposits shelved in the 1980s-90s at $350-400 gold look very different.
  • For a panner: one gram of gold is worth about $134. Wisconsin placer gold is almost all flour-size, so a good day is usually a few specks.

Rules that matter

  • Recreational panning needs no DNR permit if it uses hand tools only (pan, shovel, screen, small hand sluice, metal detector), is not for sale, and moves less than 2 cubic yards of streambed per waterway per year. Anything with a motor (dredge, powered excavation) needs a prospecting permit.
  • Private land: riverbank owners own to the middle of the stream, including what's in the streambed. Get permission first.
  • No collecting in state parks, state trails, state recreation areas, State Wild Rivers (including the Pine and Popple in Florence County), State Natural Areas, or state-owned lakebeds. Other DNR land may need a collector's permit (5 lb a day, 50 lb a year). For national forest land, ask the Forest Service.
  • Mining law: the 2017 repeal of the "Prove It First" law ended Wisconsin's effective sulfide-mining moratorium. A 2025-26 bill on sulfide mining permits (SB 623 / AB 632) failed on March 23, 2026, so the 2017 rules still stand.
  • Treaty rights: much of northern Wisconsin is in the 1837 and 1842 Ojibwe ceded territories, where tribes keep hunting, fishing and gathering rights. Tribes have opposed Reef, Crandon and Back Forty, so any real mining proposal should expect that.

What still could not be reached

  • Parcel ownership (sco.wisc.edu): needed to check each pit.
  • River-level statistics: the USGS water site loads, but its data comes from api.waterdata.usgs.gov, which is blocked. In general, Wisconsin rivers run lowest in late summer to early fall, the best time to pan.
  • Old newspapers (loc.gov) block automated searches, and mindat.org, sec.gov and the legislature site were also unreachable.

Sources: GreenLight Metals Reef and Bend pages; Bend drilling approval, Feb 2026; 2026 strategy; Bend results, July 2026; Lobo projects; WI DNR mining projects; WI DNR gold panning rules; Pine-Popple Wild Rivers; SB 623 status; gold price Oct 16, 2026; GLIFWC; Macrostrat; WPR on GreenLight permits.

Streams most likely to carry gold

Every one of Wisconsin's ~258,000 mapped stream segments (USGS high-resolution NHD) was scored. Each gold source (known deposits, Tier A-C targets, USGS gold, arsenic and antimony highs, LiDAR pits, historic placer and mine reports) was snapped to the nearest channel and carried downstream, with the signal halving every 20 km. Segments were then weighted for bedrock setting, stream size (orders 3-6 hold the most gravel) and nearby faults or the Niagara suture. Along the top reaches, the 10 m USGS elevation model was used to find placer traps: places where a steep stretch suddenly flattens, which is where heavy gold drops out.

These have real placer reports but sit in sandstone and glacial country, so their gold is glacial flour rather than from a nearby lode.

How to read this

  • Florence County has the strongest stream signal in the state: the Pine, Menominee and Little Popple all drain the H1, H6 and H8 highs along the Niagara suture. Treating all land as open (the working assumption for this project), the Pine River trap at 45.8286, -88.2396 is the single best panning target in the state, with the Little Popple and Menominee close behind.
  • The Yellow River system below Bend is the best-proven: it drains a deposit with confirmed gold, and its till runs 2-4 times normal gold.
  • Some "traps" are dams or lake outlets. Many dams were built on natural falls, where bedrock cracks just below the falls are classic gold catchers, but dam property is usually off-limits.
  • Best timing: late summer to early fall low water. Work the inside of bends, the downstream end of gravel bars, and bedrock cracks below riffles.

Data: USGS NHD High Resolution, Wisconsin · USGS 3DEP 1/3 arc-second DEM · all earlier layers in this doc.

Satellite iron-stain scan: no usable targets

The statewide leaf-off photos were scanned for rusty red-orange bare ground around Florence, Bend, the Taylor till belt, Reef, Penokee and the Vilas hotspot. Every strong patch, checked up close, was brown sedge marsh, dead grass, plowed fields, red-twigged shrubs or a pond edge. Color photos alone cannot separate iron-stained rock from vegetation here. True mineral mapping needs Sentinel-2 infrared bands, and that image server (sentinel-cogs.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com) is still blocked.

Data: WI DNR imagery and parcel services · USGS Water Data API · Earth Search Sentinel-2 catalog

Fourth pass: old USGS reports, the state gold list and satellite infrared

What the old reports added

  • New Florence target, FS (about 45.827, -88.228; sections 27/34, T39N R18E, located to about 1 km). USGS Professional Paper 633 (1971) reports drill holes there that cut slate with pyrrhotite and pyrite veinlets, along a northwest magnetic belt whose strongest peak (6,750 gammas) was never explained. It sits right on the Niagara suture. Now ranked 4th.
  • H6 drops slightly. The same report says a drill hole about 1 km away (section 36) hit hematite-magnetite iron formation, the likely cause of H6's strong magnetic high. Iron formation along a suture can still host gold, so H6 stays in Tier A.
  • Florence was heavily prospected for iron (Little Commonwealth, Dunkel, St. Clair, Dickey, Welch, Ernst, Spread Eagle). Some LiDAR pits may be iron test pits; their dumps are still free bedrock samples.
  • The 1985 state gold list (WGNHS OFR 1985-05) adds the Pelican River massive-sulfide deposit (sec. 29, T36N R10E, near Rhinelander; about 45.566, -89.274). It is now Tier B, and the Pelican River enters the top-20 stream list at #14.
  • The Reef thesis (WGNHS OFR 1988-08) shows Reef-type gold travels with copper and zinc, with almost no arsenic (up to 590 ppb gold beside quartz veins in mafic volcanics; volcanic rocks there carry 12 times normal gold). Copper highs on volcanic rock now count more in the scoring; arsenic and antimony remain the clue for Florence-style gold.
  • USGS Professional Paper 513 (1966) covers the Menominee iron district east of Florence. No gold is reported, but it confirms Big and Little Quinnesec Falls on the Menominee are exposed volcanic bedrock.

Dams versus natural traps

All stream trap points were checked against the national dams inventory. Natural traps: Pine River, Little Popple, Menominee below Quinnesec (45.7579, -87.9402), Yellow River (Bend), Black River, Eau Claire River (Reef), Washington Creek, Brunsweiler, White, Marengo and Pelican rivers. Dam sites: Big and Little Quinnesec Falls, Chequamegon Waters, Rest Lake, Thornapple, Ladysmith, Wausau, Rothschild, DuBay, Grandmother, Tomahawk and Turtle-Flambeau. The stream map now shows natural traps in gold and dam traps in gray.

Sentinel-2 infrared scan: no bedrock alteration visible

Three clear leaf-off scenes per area (2019-2026) were combined to map clay and iron-oxide ratios on bare ground around Florence, Bend, the Taylor till belt, Reef and Penokee. Only 2-20% of each area is bare. Every clay-plus-iron spot checked on aerial photos was a wetland, beaver meadow, pond edge, plowed field or sandy clearing. Glacial cover and forest hide the bedrock, so satellite alteration mapping does not work here; ground sampling is the way forward.

Sources: USGS Professional Paper 633 (Dutton, 1971, Geology of the Florence Area) with plates; USGS Geophysical Investigations Map GP-576 (1966); USGS Professional Paper 513 (1966); WGNHS Open-File Reports 1985-05 and 1988-08; National Inventory of Dams; Earth Search Sentinel-2.
