Newspaper leads (1902). The Wisconsin Blue Book chronology for 1902 says: "Finds of gold were reported near Prairie du Chien in January, in Polk County in August, and in Dunn County in October." Dunn County borders Eau Claire County and drains to the Red Cedar and Chippewa rivers. Polk County sits on the copper-bearing St. Croix volcanics. The Prairie du Chien report is on limestone and was most likely pyrite (fool's gold). A 1919 Manitowoc Herald clipping titled "Fool's gold" (Kaukauna) is the same kind of false alarm. The places for the Polk and Dunn finds still need the original articles: try the Menomonie Dunn County News for October 1902 and the St. Croix Falls or Osceola papers for August 1902. Most other gold stories in the uploaded pages (Klondike, British Columbia, "Bonanza Kings", Black Hills, the Sumpter, Oregon company) are about western mines, not Wisconsin.

Source: Wisconsin Blue Book, chronology p. 866 (UW Digital Collections); Wisconsin Historical Society clipping BA7134.

Lost treasure and metal detecting

The project now covers lost caches, robbery loot, payroll gold and old town sites too. Every event is on the interactive Wisconsin Lost Treasure Map. Each marker has the story, the value, whether it was found, the source, where to look, and a Google Maps link. Marker color shows how reliable the story is: documented record, newspaper story, legend, or forum rumor. New newspaper articles go straight onto that map.

Starting set: 32 events. These are the ones that matter most:

  • Kraft State Bank robbery, Menomonie (1931). This is a real, documented crime about 25 minutes from Eau Claire. The gang got away with $90,000, and no source says the money was recovered.
  • Neillsville silver jar (found 1962). A real find: $56.30 in 1800s silver coins in a fruit jar inside a pail, 18 inches down, on a farm 3 miles west of Neillsville. Farm caches usually look like this.
  • Muddy Creek near Elk Mound ($35,000 in gold coins along a fence line) and Hurlburt's money in the Rush River valley. Both are close to home, but both are forum rumors with no source found yet.
  • Whitehall treasure cave (1924), Brisbois gold at Prairie du Chien (1924), and a Wisconsin River bluff cave in Richland County (1923). Real newspaper articles held by the Wisconsin Historical Society. The archive shows only the headlines, so screenshots of their page images would fill in the details.
  • Dillinger's suitcase at Little Bohemia (1934), Apostle Islands caches, Fort Crawford payroll gold. These are the famous legends. They are well known and well searched.

Off limits whatever the scenario: burial mounds, graves and cemeteries. Wisconsin's burial-sites law protects them, and they are left out of the map on purpose. Objects 50 or more years old found on state land must stay where they are found, and everywhere else needs the landowner's permission.

Sources: TreasureSeekr, TreasureNet forum, Kraft State Bank robbery, Clark County Press 1962, Wisconsin Historical Society clippings (BA10718, BA10721, BA3551), WI DNR metal detecting rules.

Newspaper gold reports (first batch of uploads, 1873–1965). Thirty newspaper pages yielded 16 Wisconsin gold reports, now on the treasure map. The rest were western or foreign mines (Cripple Creek, Manitoba, Manila, Haiti, Minnesota). The cluster that matters most is west of Eau Claire:

  • Dunn County, three separate reports: Knapp (1901, Sam Tufts, about $3 a ton plus silver and copper), a well in the town of Lucas near Menomonie (1903, $145 a ton over 85 feet), and an Eau Galle gold mine in the early 1900s that sold shares locally. Together with the 1902 Blue Book item, this makes Dunn County the most reported gold county in the uploads.
  • St. Croix and Pierce counties: a real gold nugget found on the Barlow farm 8 miles south of Hudson (1906), gold-bearing well sands near River Falls (1906), and the Plum Creek shaft with traces of gold and platinum.
  • Big Falls, Eau Claire River: a 1965 history column confirms a 30-foot shaft worked in 1896, with a later test of about $20 a ton. This backs up the Big Falls (BF) target.
  • Barron County (1948): Clayton Seevers panned gold in a creek in the town of Dovre near New Auburn and filed a 40-acre claim on the Solberg farm. A University of Wisconsin metallurgist confirmed his samples contained gold, and two other prospectors staked claims nearby (Kenosha Evening News, Jul 14 1948).
  • Pepin (1909): a 40-foot shaft on the Heinenman farm, claimed over $150 a ton in copper, gold and silver.

The Prairie du Chien 1902 report turned out to be the Dousman "gold quartz" in limestone, so it stays low priority.

Taylor County was mined underground in 1887. The Chippewa Falls Herald (Apr 8, 1887), quoting the Medford Star and News, says Taylor County mining crews were working at Chelsea, Medford and Pine Creek and expected to reach ore before the next snow. In the same column, Chas. Powell brought in gold-bearing quartz that showed free gold in an assay, and he claimed to know where the ledge was. This backs up the Taylor till-gold belt (TB) target, about 25 km from Bend. Old shafts near Chelsea and Pine Creek are the next thing to look for on LiDAR.

Panning gravel pits and trucked-in material

Does material trucked in from out of state carry gold?

Mostly no, with one big exception: the glaciers already did the trucking.

  • Crushed quarry rock (driveway rock, road base, rail ballast, riprap, trap rock from Dresser) is broken bedrock. It never sat in a stream, so it has no placer gold. Skip it.
  • Washed decorative river rock from gold states (Montana, Colorado) did come from rivers, but it is screened to size and washed. The fines, where flour gold rides, are gone, and the big cobbles never held any. The odds are close to zero.
  • Glacial sand and gravel is the real "imported" material. The ice sheets hauled rock from Canada and the Lake Superior basin and dropped it here. Meltwater then sorted it, so the heavy minerals (magnetite, garnet and gold) gather at the bottom of each gravel layer. Every local gravel pit is a pile of out-of-state rock already sorted by water, and this is where Wisconsin flour gold is found. The Minnesota DNR sampled sand and gravel pits for exactly this reason: to see whether pits mined for aggregate also hold heavy minerals worth recovering.
  • Store-bought paydirt (Alaska, Klondike, Colorado bags) is a real, guaranteed way to pan real gold at home. You pay roughly what the gold is worth. Buy from sellers that state the gold weight, since some bags are salted.

Gravel pits and wash plants near Eau Claire

The Wisconsin Lost Treasure Map now has 19 sand and gravel pits and plants within about 30 km, from the USGS mineral database, under the kind "Gravel pit or wash plant". They fall in two groups:

  • Chippewa River outwash (Shawtown, south Eau Claire, Pit No. 4, Brunswick, Hallie, Plant No. 2, Custer, Lane, Colony, Perrenoud, Lake Pit, Caryville, Coon Creek, Talford). These gravels came down the Chippewa and Flambeau from the north, past the Flambeau gold-copper deposit at Ladysmith. This is the best-sourced gravel in the area.
  • Red Cedar and Elk Creek gravel (Elk Creek pits, Elk Mound, Muddy Creek, Townline Road). The Muddy Creek pit sits near the Muddy Creek fence-line gold legend.

How to work a pit: with the operator's permission, pan the fine sand from the screen deck or the wash-plant settling pond, and any dark black-sand streaks low on the pit face. Bring a magnet to pull magnetite out of the black sand. Several of these records date from the 1990s, so check a current aerial photo before driving out.

Documented panning streams within 2 hours

  • Rock Elm and Plum Creeks (Pierce County): worked as placers in 1887–1890, with diamonds also found. A 1985 program confirmed the gold but never found its source.
  • St. Croix Dalles and the drift north of St. Croix Falls (Polk County): WGNHS reports flakes and nuggets in basalt crevices at the Dalles, and flakes in the glacial drift north of town.
  • Big Falls (Eau Claire River) and Knapp (Dunn County) are already on the map.

Clubs: the Wausau Prospectors (GPAA, first Saturday monthly, (715) 340-2831) and the Twin Cities Prospectors (GPAA, (612) 245-6569) pan Wisconsin creeks and know the local spots.

Real-world rules, for reference: the Wisconsin DNR allows hand panning and small hand sluices without a permit if you move less than 2 cubic yards per stream per year. Powered dredges need permits, and the streambed belongs to the landowner. In real life, collecting is banned in state parks and on state Wild and Scenic rivers; this plan treats those as open under the project scenario.

Sources: WI DNR gold panning; WGNHS gold in Wisconsin; MN DNR heavy minerals in sand and gravel pits; USGS MRDS; Wausau Prospectors; Twin Cities Prospectors; CBS Minnesota on prospecting.

More treasure leads within 2 hours

Added to the treasure map: the Black River forks near Hatfield (French-buried gold artifacts, forum rumor), Lake Pepin Spanish gold and the 1686 French post Fort Saint Antoine, the St. Croix fur traders' gold, the Winona gang's loot, Capone's Hideout at Cranberry Lake, the Portage riverboat gold bars, and 15 ghost towns in Eau Claire, Dunn, Clark, Jackson, Trempealeau and Buffalo counties. The Kraft State Bank robbery entry now includes the escape route (east on U.S. 12, north on County B, east on Suckow Road) and the abandoned farms where the gang stashed gas and left a dying member with some of the securities.

Less obvious spots (third pass)

The treasure map now opens on the area within about 2 hours of Eau Claire, with a dashed ring for that distance. Marker color shows what a spot is (treasure, gold and panning, gravel pits, beaches and landings, old towns and camps). Faded markers are legends or rumors, and the WI button shows the whole state. These 20 spots were added:

Dam and falls bedrock (gold). Flour gold rides with black sand and gets trapped in cracked bedrock in fast water. Below a dam or falls, the river has scoured down to bedrock. Spots: Dells Dam in Eau Claire, the falls at Chippewa Falls, Jim Falls, Cornell (Brunet Falls), Holcombe (the first big trap below the Flambeau gold-copper deposit), and Cedar Falls on the Red Cedar. Work these at low water, crevice-clean the cracks, and try moss mining: strip the moss off rocks at the high-water line and wash it in a tub. Moss catches flour gold during floods.

Lower Chippewa gravel bars below Durand. Big bars reshuffled every spring, with black sand at the head of each bar and behind snags. These bars also produce Lake Superior agates, near the 1800s gold reports at Durand.

Where people lost things for a century:

  • Beef Slough at Alma (1867–1909): every log from the Chippewa pinery was sorted and rafted here, with 1,200–1,500 men in season, 75 rowboats and thousands of pilings. Rivermen lost coins, knives, peaveys and boom chains along the slough.
  • Reads Landing, Minnesota: where the rafts were combined and the pilots met.
  • Eau Claire steamboat landings and Water Street (1850s–1890s): the landing at 4th Avenue and Water Street and Kelsey Landing, in the old saloon district.
  • Half Moon Lake beach: Eau Claire's swimming beach for over a century. Water hunting at waist depth finds the most rings. Also Lake Wissota and Lake Altoona beaches.
  • Northern Wisconsin State Fair grounds, Chippewa Falls: fairs every year since 1897.
  • Six CCC camps from 1933–1941: Camp Globe and Camp Fairchild (Fairchild), Camp Nelson, Camp Perkinstown, Camp Mondeaux and Camp Rusk. Each held about 200 men. Look for the barracks rows on 1938 aerial photos, and the camp dump in a nearby ravine.

Still kept off the map: burial mounds, graves and cemeteries.

Sources: WGNHS gold in Wisconsin; Beef Slough Boom and Improvement; Alma Historical Society on Beef Slough; Eau Claire steamboat landings; Half Moon Lake swimming, 1916; Northern Wisconsin State Fair; UW-Eau Claire CCC camp newsletters.

Separate metal detecting map

The Chippewa Valley Detecting Map covers the area within about an hour of Eau Claire. It holds 40 places where people gathered and dropped things, sorted into five kinds: beaches and swimming holes, gathering places, crossings and landings, work camps and mills, and vanished towns. Each spot says why it works and how to hunt it. The less obvious ones:

  • Electric Park (Midway Park), 1895–1920s: an amusement park between Eau Claire and Chippewa Falls on the interurban line, with rides, a dance pavilion, a band shell and a ball park. Its exact spot is disputed, so pin it down before hunting.
  • Stardusk Drive-In (1949–1983), County OO: drive-in lots are coin carpets, because change falls out every time a car door opens.
  • The old county fairgrounds: Augusta (1924–1939), Fall Creek (early 1930s) and Altoona (1941–1996). Depression-era fairs mean silver coins.
  • The interurban line (1898–1926) and its Irvine Park loop, where people waited for cars.
  • Ferry landings: the 1856 Gage and Reed ferry downtown, and the Caryville ferry, which carried up to 300 cars a day until 1964.
  • Big Falls swimming hole: jewelry and flour gold in the same bedrock cracks.
  • Dells Mill (1864): farmers waited there for hours with their wagons.
Old river channels and glacial deposits

I built a height-above-river model of the Chippewa valley from USGS 10 m elevation data. On it, abandoned channels and meander scars show up as low ground just above today's rivers. The higher green benches are glacial outwash terraces: dry riverbeds from the meltwater era.

Old channels (O1–O6 on the image):

  • O1: an abandoned meander loop below Chippewa Falls.
  • O2: the low terrace and old channel at Lake Hallie.
  • O3: the Wissota terrace, the high outwash plain toward Bloomer.
  • O4: meander scars in the Caryville bottoms.
  • O5: Half Moon Lake, a cut-off loop of the Chippewa.
  • O6: a meltwater valley into the Yellow River at Cadott.

When a river moves, the heavy bottom gravel where gold sits is left behind, usually under a few feet of sand or silt.

Glacial deposits from Syverson's Chippewa County bulletin:

  • the Chippewa and Jump River diversion channels at Cornell and Holcombe
  • the Otter Lake tunnel channel and esker; an esker is the gravel bed of a river that ran inside the ice, a natural sluice
  • the Chippewa Moraine boulder country, with dry channels on the Plummer Lake plain
  • the front of the Perkinstown moraine
  • the Bob Lake ice-walled-lake delta
  • the older River Falls outwash in western Chippewa County, which carries red Lake Superior basalt and large agates from the copper country

All of these are on the treasure map under "Gold, panning, old channels".

Glacial boulders and gold

An erratic boulder by itself rarely holds gold. Most are granite or gneiss. Boulders matter in three other ways:

  • Boulder lags. Where meltwater or a river washed the sand and silt away, boulders were left in piles or pavements. The heavy minerals stayed with them, so dig under and between the boulders in a lag.
  • Indicator boulders ("float"). A boulder of rusty quartz vein, greenstone with pyrite, or banded iron formation is a piece of the kind of rock that carries gold. Break it, crush a sample, and pan it. A train of similar boulders points back up-ice (north to northeast here) toward where it came from.
  • Boulders in streams. Every big boulder in a creek makes a low-pressure eddy behind it, and gold settles in the gravel at its downstream foot and in the crack where boulder meets bedrock.

Best boulder country nearby: the Chippewa Moraine south of New Auburn, the Perkinstown moraine from Otter Lake to Cornell, and the till plains around Seevers' 1948 gold creek near New Auburn.

Reading a river: what to look for

Where gold settles:

  • Inside bends: the slow side of a curve, at the upstream (head) end of the gravel bar.
  • Behind obstacles: the downstream side of boulders, logs and bridge piers, where the current drops.
  • Bedrock: cracks, potholes and riffles in exposed bedrock, especially below falls and dams. Gold works down into them over centuries.
  • Where the slope flattens: below rapids, where a steep reach turns slow. The placer traps on the stream map are these.
  • Where a tributary enters: the main river slows at the mouth and drops what the side stream carried.
  • The high-water line: moss, grass roots and the gravel at the flood line catch fine gold. Wash the moss in a tub.
  • Bottom of the gravel: gold sits on the lowest layer, just above bedrock or a clay layer called "false bedrock".

Signs in the gravel and banks:

  • Black sand (magnetite, ilmenite): black streaks on bar heads, or a dark smear when you swirl a pan. It moves with gold, and a magnet pulls it out. More black sand means a better trap.
  • Red garnet sand: pink-red grains with black sand, another heavy-mineral sign that WGNHS names for Wisconsin gold.
  • Clay layers: blue-gray or tan clay under gravel acts as false bedrock. Gold stops on top of it. Pan the inch of gravel resting on the clay.
  • Iron staining: orange and rust-red bands in gravel banks mark old water tables and oxidized pyrite. Rusty quartz pebbles are worth a crush test.
  • Quartz: white vein quartz cobbles, especially rusty or with dark specks, come from vein rock, the source of lode gold.
  • Heavy, flat cobbles packed together: a tight cobble pavement means fast water sorted it, and fines got trapped underneath.
  • Red Lake Superior basalt and agates: a sign the gravel came from the Lake Superior copper country.

What fools people: pyrite ("fool's gold") is brassy and shatters; mica flakes are gold-colored but float and look gold only at one angle; weathered brass and lead shot turn up near towns. Real gold stays yellow in shade, bends without breaking, and sinks fast.

Sources: Syverson 2007, Pleistocene Geology of Chippewa County (WGNHS B103); WI DNR Chippewa Moraine geology; WGNHS gold in Wisconsin; USGS 3DEP elevation; Electric Park; Chippewa Valley Electric Railway; Stardusk Drive-In; 100 years of the Eau Claire County Fair; Caryville ferry; Carson Park.

The big picture: six theories

Combining every layer in this doc points to six testable theories; the strongest is a single telluride-rich gold district around Wausau that links Reef, the old Eason shaft, the Wausau pegmatite gold and model targets T1 and T3. The odds are my judgment of whether a first cheap test finds anomalous gold, not a calculation.

More spots and five new ideas

Ten overlooked spots from the data plus five new ideas; the top pick is model target T2 near Lynne, which scored nearly as high as the ground beside Reef and is not held by a company.

The five new ideas:

  • Flambeau dispersal train: glaciers scraped Flambeau's gold-rich top and spread it down-ice; till and gravel just southwest of Ladysmith may carry that trail, a known source to calibrate your panning against.
  • Jump River gravels: the river cuts through the belt between Flambeau and Bend; pan bars below Big Falls near Kennan.
  • Wisconsin River trail: it drains Lynne, Pelican River and the Price–Lincoln chain before Wausau; pan at the Wisconsin River Forest Landing and compare with the Chippewa trail.
  • Big Eau Pleine drawdown: the reservoir drains the Eau Pleine shear zone and target T6; winter drawdowns expose old channel gravels.
  • Merrill outwash pits: gravel pits south of the Price–Lincoln chain work outwash from belt rock; ask to pan wash-plant fines.

Five more ideas (round 2):

  • Twig chemistry over till: tree roots reach through thick till; explorers in Canada assay spruce and balsam twigs for gold and pathfinders. Try it along the Taylor fault corridor (T5, T7).
  • Lake-bottom mud: small lakes collect fine sediment from their whole watershed; a few mud cores from lakes between Lynne and Rhinelander screen many square miles.
  • Beaver dams as sluices: beaver ponds slow streams and drop heavy grains; pan gravel just below old dams on creeks in the Price County gap.
  • Railroad cuts and rights: Bend's mineral rights belong to the Soo Line Railroad, so old rail land grants may hold other belt mineral rights; rail cuts also expose rock. Check deed records along the line.
  • Thornapple below Eisenbrey: the Thornapple River runs past the Eisenbrey copper-gold deposit before joining the Flambeau; pan the first bars downstream.
Railroad cuts

Only two railroad rock cuts are documented in the reports reached: one through the Eau Pleine shear zone west of Meyer's Landing (44.710° N, 89.699° W) (MDPI), and a granite cut near Beck Tower wayside south of Monico (WGNHS). The other points are rail stretches crossing high-scoring belt ground, worth scouting for cuts from public crossings or rail-trails only.

Meteorites and impact craters

Meteorites are not a gold source: they hold only about 0.1–4 ppm gold, below ore grade and worth far more to collectors as meteorites (Detector Prospector summary). The real link is impact craters, whose hot-water systems can form or preserve ore, as at Sudbury and possibly the Witwatersrand (ANU).

Wisconsin has two impact structures and 14 recorded meteorites (WGNHS, UW-Madison, Wikipedia). Rock Elm beside Plum Creek is the only one that pairs an impact with confirmed gold; the Trenton strewn field east of West Bend is the best place to hunt meteorites themselves.

Beyond Rock Elm and Glover Bluff: Brussels Hill in Door County is the leading Wisconsin candidate (Live Science); Decorah, Iowa is a probable crater just over the line; Calvin (MI), Des Plaines and Glasford (IL), Manson (IA) and the Slate Islands (ON) are confirmed nearby (Wikipedia list). A circular area between Eau Claire and La Crosse has been proposed but shows no impact evidence (Wisconsin Geology blog).

Why each area

1. Reef shear corridor. Reef is orogenic gold, the style behind most of the world's gold output, trapped where the northeast-trending Eau Claire River fault cuts the Eau Pleine shear zone, a major terrane boundary (GreenLight). Orogenic deposits sit on lower-order faults off crustal-scale shears (USGS), so other splays along the Eau Pleine zone are the logical next look. A 1988 survey study found gold up to 590 ppb along the shear and saw shearing fade eastward from the river (WGNHS). Note: this Eau Claire River is in Marathon County, not the one in Eau Claire.

2. Ladysmith–Bend corridor. This western end of the belt hosts Flambeau, Eisenbrey (Thornapple), Bend and Ritchie Creek (Mindat, Mindat). VMS deposits cluster on the same volcanic horizons, and GreenLight's 2025 Bend holes all hit copper-gold mineralization (GreenLight). Glacial cover is the main reason gaps between them stay untested.

3. Rhinelander–Crandon district. Crandon is the belt's largest deposit, and Lynne, Pelican River, Horseshoe and Hawk sit nearby (Mines.edu thesis, Mindat). Past work chased zinc and copper; gold-rich zones within or beside these systems have had little attention.

4. Beecher–Pembine greenstone. East-west quartz veins cutting greenstone and gabbro at Archie, and the Miscauno shaft east of Beecher, show gold-bearing fluids moved here (WGNHS gold). Both are small and old, which is exactly why the area is untested by modern methods.

5. Northern Superior margin. The state survey records reported gold at the Northern Belle Mine and exploration in T45N R4W, plus gold-copper-silver values in conglomerate at Davis Hill (WGNHS gold, WGNHS 1985). Evidence is thin, but new survey data now covers part of it.

6. Placers near Eau Claire. St. Croix Dalles is the only documented placer production; Big Falls on the Eau Claire River and the Cumberland nuggets are poorly documented and may be fraudulent (WGNHS 1985). Worth a weekend pan, not a claim.

How to test them

Start from free public geophysics and old drill records, then go to the ground only where the two agree.

  1. Pull the new airborne data. USGS Earth MRI released high-resolution magnetic and radiometric surveys over the Upper Peninsula and parts of northern Wisconsin from 2025 flights (ScienceBase), alongside a 2021 electromagnetic survey of northeast Wisconsin (USGS). Trace linear magnetic highs off the Eau Pleine and Eau Claire River structures, and conductors on known volcanic horizons.
  2. Check what was already drilled. The state survey's annual exploration summaries from 1980–1984 list every licensed company and where it drilled (WGNHS 1982). Anomalies with no nearby holes are the real gaps.
  3. Sample carefully through the till. A USGS study at Bend found stacked till sheets from distant sources masked the deposit's signal (USGS). Basal till or drilling beats surface soil here.
  4. Sort out mineral rights. Bend's rights are leased from the Soo Line Railroad on national forest land (WPR), and GreenLight holds a state exploration license through June 2027 (DNR). Every target needs its own rights check before any work.

Open question: whether GreenLight or others already hold leases along the Reef corridor beyond the project itself.

Along-strike targets off the Reef shear zone

Inferred from published magnetic interpretations and old reports, not from the raw grids, which this workspace could not download. Treat every row as a hypothesis to check against the Earth MRI data.

Reef sits in sections 25–36, T29N R9E (Town of Easton), on the western edge of the Eau Claire River shear zone, mapped about 3 km wide (WGNHS 1988). Its host unit is traced about 2,400 m along a northeast trend and is open along strike and down-dip (GreenLight).

What to check in the raw data, once it can be downloaded:

  • Trace the linear magnetic highs at Reef and follow them both ways along strike
  • Mark where northeast splays cross magnetic mafic volcanic units (likely gold traps)
  • Overlay the 1980s drillhole locations to find splays never drilled
  • Use radiometric potassium highs to flag possible alteration along the shears
Magnetic data results

The USGS magnetic grid puts Reef inside a narrow magnetic corridor trending about 30° east of north, squeezed between two large magnetic bodies. Magnetic contacts on that same trend continue at least 24 km southwest and 11 km northeast of Reef.

Data: the USGS 1 km merged aeromagnetic grid for the U.S. (USGS), processed into a residual field (15 km regional trend removed) and a tilt derivative, whose zero line (black) traces magnetic contacts. I checked its positions against the independent USGS 2 km grid: the two agree within about 1 km (correlation 0.73). A 1 km cell cannot see Reef's 1–5 m veins; it maps the structures that host them.

The body east of Reef is a ring-shaped magnetic complex. That fits USGS mapping of highly magnetic circular anorthosite plutons inside the Wolf River batholith (USGS). Reef sits on the contact zone along its western edge.

A higher-resolution pass needs the North-central Wisconsin survey (0.8 km lines), which is hosted by the state survey, and the 2025 Earth MRI data. Both sites (wgnhs.wisc.edu and sciencebase.gov) are still blocked from this workspace.

Does the belt extend further?

Yes, in places. The belt already reaches Michigan, where Back Forty sits at its east end (Mines.edu thesis). Minnesota's survey says Wisconsin's volcanic belts may have counterparts there (Minnesota Geological Survey). The magnetic fabric also suggests belt-like crust continues south under the sandstone, but magnetics alone can't prove those rocks are the same ore-bearing volcanics.

The table compares each test area with the known belt (area 1). "ENE share" is the fraction of the area whose magnetic grain trends 45–100°; "texture" is the spread of the residual field, a rough measure of how varied the buried rock is.

AreaMean trendENE shareTexture (nT)Reading
1 Known belt, WI68°70%203Baseline
2 Central WI, south of belt65°64%187Nearly identical to the belt; this is the Marshfield terrane south of the Eau Pleine suture
3 South-central WI, under sandstone57°78%133Same grain, muted by deeper cover
4 East-central Minnesota, buried40°47%186Different grain; partial match
5 Upper Peninsula, Michigan91°62%800Known extension; strong iron-rich rocks

What that suggests:

  • Central Wisconsin (area 2) is the strongest lead: its magnetic grain and texture nearly match the belt, it lies just south of the Reef corridor, and its cover is thin. It is a different terrane (an older microcontinent), so volcanic rocks there would need confirming by drill core.
  • Under the sandstone (area 3) the grain continues, but this crust lies south of the Spirit Lake tectonic zone, a younger suture (EarthArXiv). It is likely younger crust, and deep cover makes it impractical for now.
  • Minnesota (area 4) matches only partly; the Minnesota survey's own drill-core library is the way to test it.

Caveat: these trends reflect any magnetic rock, not only volcanics. The next step is to check old drill-hole logs in each area, at the Wisconsin and Minnesota survey core libraries, before ranking them as targets.

Stalled and overlooked prospects

The biggest overlooked lead is Kennecott's 1967 airborne survey around Ladysmith: it logged about 140 conductive anomalies, and only two (Flambeau and Thornapple) were ever confirmed as deposits (WGNHS 1979). Between the late 1960s and 1991, companies outlined nearly 90 million tons of massive sulfide at eight Wisconsin localities, and none reached production except Flambeau (OneMine). Exploration then stalled in the 1980s bust and the 1998 moratorium, leaving known prospects undrilled for decades.

Same belt, between two proven deposits, little public drilling since

In 2024 the county board weighed opening county land to mining inquiries; gold is a minor byproduct

DuvalMarinette (T35–36N, R18E)Duval Corp., 1971–74, found by airborne survey: ~10 million tons of pyrrhotite-rich sulfide in iron formation, nearly barren of base and precious metals (WGNHS)No metal valueLow for gold. A warning: strong airborne conductors near the Beecher–Pembine area can be barren sulfide

Two lessons for targeting:

  • Magnetics alone will miss some deposits. Crandon had no magnetic signature at the survey spacing used, so electromagnetic (EM) surveys, which detect conductive sulfides, are the right follow-up tool for this deposit style.
  • Ownership varies parcel by parcel. Private land around these prospects is open to leasing, but mineral rights are often split from the surface, so check each parcel at the county register of deeds.
Bedrock windows on the ground

Most of the belt is buried under glacial sediment, so waterfalls, rapids and gorges are the rare places where the bedrock shows at the surface. Locations are from Google Maps; most are public parks where collecting is not allowed.

SiteCoordinatesWhy it matters
Dells of the Eau Claire County Park45.006° N, 89.337° WBedrock gorge about 4 miles north of Reef, on the Eau Claire River shear zone; the best place to see Reef-type rocks
Big Falls County Park, Eau Claire River44.821° N, 91.293° WSite of the rumored 1930 placer pit in the riverbed; closest to Eau Claire
Big Falls, Jump River, Kennan45.407° N, 90.641° WRapids over belt rocks between Flambeau and Bend
Twelve Foot Falls Park45.579° N, 88.137° WExposed rocks near the Duval deposit and the Pembine area
Long Slide Falls County Park45.685° N, 87.934° WNear the Niagara fault and the Archie gold veins
Rib Mountain State Park44.922° N, 89.688° WQuartzite hill above the Wausau plain; shows the rocks around the Reef corridor

Terrain clues to look for on topographic maps:

  • Straight river reaches and aligned lakes often follow faults. The Eau Claire River runs along the shear zone named after it.
  • Falls and rapids mark bedrock at the surface, and their plunge pools are natural traps for heavy minerals, including placer gold.
  • Rusty seeps and orange-stained wetlands can mark weathering sulfides underneath; under thick glacial cover they are rare, so any you find near the targets are worth sampling.
  • Eskers and outwash gravels downstream (south and southwest) of the belt are where glaciers dumped crushed rock, and the best places to pan.

Open question: a true terrain analysis needs elevation data from epqs.nationalmap.gov or elevation.nationalmap.gov, which this workspace can't reach yet.

Straight lines: possible faults

The clearest fault-like lines in the belt are a cluster of five northeast-trending magnetic lines just southwest of Reef, the same direction as the fault that controls Reef's gold. That cluster is Target A.

Method: I traced magnetic contacts in the USGS 1 km grid and kept those running straight for at least 10 km (212 lines). Orange lines trend northeast like Reef's fault; purple lines follow the belt's east-northeast grain. I then flagged river stretches that run straight for 8 km or more along a magnetic line, using Natural Earth river outlines (Natural Earth).

#RiverApprox. locationLengthWhat it suggests
1Flambeau45.85°–45.91° N, 90.61°–90.45° W14.5 kmRuns along an east-northeast magnetic line near the belt's northern edge; possibly following the Niagara fault zone
3Flambeau45.75°–45.82° N, 90.78°–90.71° W9.8 kmSame line, just downstream; together, about 25 km of the river may follow one structure
2Namekagon46.04°–46.14° N, 91.46°–91.39° W12.6 kmIn Midcontinent Rift rocks, a copper setting outside the gold belt
4Red Cedar44.96°–45.00° N, 91.89°–91.80° W9.1 kmWest of the belt; low priority

The Flambeau River reaches (1 and 3) are the most interesting river lines: they sit just north of the belt's mapped edge, upstream of the Flambeau mine. Caveat: the river outlines are simplified for small-scale maps, so some straightness may be an artifact. A detailed elevation or hydrography check would confirm them.

Big Falls placer area

Best guess: the 1930 pit was in the bedrock channel at or just below Big Falls, around 44.817° N, 91.295° W. The 1985 state list puts it in the center of the Eau Claire River in the SW¼ of section 13, T27N R8W, with gold rumored from crevices in the bedrock (WGNHS 1985). My conversion of that section lands about 1 km south of the main falls, within the error of a hand conversion, and bedrock crevices point to the falls themselves. The record is poorly documented and may be fraudulent.

Work the heads of gravel bars, inside bends, and the black-sand streaks after high water.

Niche clues to look for

The best low-cost clues here are chemical: Reef and Bend both carry tellurium, so tellurium, arsenic and bismuth in soil or stream samples can flag gold-bearing ground before any gold shows up (Yellow Dog Watershed, WPR).

ClueWhat to look forWhy it points to gold
Pathfinder metalsTellurium, arsenic, bismuth, antimony in a cheap multi-element lab assay of fine stream silt or basal tillReef's gold comes with telluride minerals; Bend cores carry tellurium
Rusty quartz floatWhite quartz with rusty, boxy holes where sulfides weathered outReef's gold sits in quartz-sulfide veins with pyrrhotite and pyrite
Magnetic rustRusty rock or black sand a magnet grabsPyrrhotite, a magnetic sulfide, is common in Reef ore
Black sand and garnetsHeavy dark sand with pink-red garnets in pansGold settles with them; forum panners report garnets with gold at Plum Creek (TreasureNet)
Boulder trainsA trail of sulfide-rich or vein-quartz boulders in fields and stone pilesGlaciers carried rock south and southwest, so the source lies up-ice to the north or northeast
Orange seeps and dead patchesIron-stained springs, stunted or bare ground in forestWeathering sulfides acidify water and soil
Old prospector pitsSquare pits in volcanic rock, like the Gold Diggers Area pits in T40N R11E (WGNHS 1985)Someone saw something worth digging
Shallow bedrockDriller logs that hit rock within a few feet; road cuts and quarriesThe only places you can sample rock without drilling
Uprooted trees and ant moundsSoil turned up from below the surface layerFree sampling of deeper till and broken bedrock
Private well arsenicDNR county data on wells above 10 ppb arsenic (Wisconsin DNR)Arsenic often travels with sulfides; a weak, cheap regional screen

Forum notes: panners report gold at Plum Creek (Nugget Lake County Park), the St. Croix Dalles, Big Falls crevices and flakes around Wausau (TreasureNet list). One poster says prospecting is no longer allowed on county land at the Dells of the Eau Claire (TreasureNet thread). These reports are anecdotal.

More opportunities

The cheapest new opportunity is old drill core already sitting in state storage: decades of company holes can be re-tested for gold pathfinders without drilling anything new.

OpportunityWhat it isWhy it could pay offFirst step
Re-test old drill coreThe state survey keeps a core repository at Mount Horeb, with industry access at $505 a day and portable XRF analysis at $6.34 a sample (WGNHS)1980s companies hunted zinc and copper; gold and tellurium in their core may never have been checkedAsk the samples coordinator which company core is held; match it to the 1980–87 exploration summaries (WGNHS 1987)
Deposits hidden under the sandstone edgeFlambeau sat under a Cambrian sandstone caprock and kept a supergene-enriched zone about 300 ft deep (WGNHS 1979)Where belt rocks dip under thin sandstone along the belt's south edge, other deposits may keep rich weathered tops that glaciers scraped off elsewhereOverlay sandstone outliers on the belt's south edge; test with EM, which sees through sandstone
New federal survey dataUSGS flew high-resolution magnetic and radiometric surveys over the Upper Peninsula and parts of northern Wisconsin in 2025 (ScienceBase), plus a 2026 helicopter EM survey of the Lake Superior basin (USGS)EM finds conductive sulfides like Flambeau and Crandon; whoever reads it first gets first pickDownload and interpret as soon as released
Northeast corner of the beltThe Fence copper prospect (chalcopyrite, pyrrhotite) in Florence County at 45.760° N, 88.570° W (Mindat), near the Back Forty trendSame terrane as the main belt, little public work, and inside the new survey areaCheck the new magnetic data around it
Lake Superior black sandFine gold reported in beach and creek sands along the south shore (TreasureNet)Placer only, but easy accessWeekend panning test

Caveat: pXRF is good for pathfinders like arsenic and copper but too insensitive for low gold levels, so send the best intervals to a fire-assay lab.

Hidden gold in the USGS prospect database

The USGS Mineral Resources Data System lists five prospects in a 55 km east–west chain across Price and Lincoln counties, and three of them carry gold or electrum, the natural gold-silver alloy (USGS MRDS). The chain sits inside the Price County gap the state survey flagged in 1979.

The same database adds two eastern prospects with gold listed as a byproduct: Mole Lake (45.498° N, 89.013° W) and Catwillow (45.629° N, 88.549° W), both in Forest County. It also corrects Bend's position to 45.295° N, 90.596° W, fixed on the updated map.

Reading: Hawk and Horseshoe were logged as zinc-copper prospects even though gold minerals were seen in them, which is exactly the kind of gold earlier explorers were not chasing.

Creative angles

These are my own inferences, untested:

  • Gravel plant fines. Washing plants at sand and gravel pits concentrate heavy minerals in their fines and settling ponds. With an owner's permission, panning those fines samples thousands of tons of glacial gravel at once.
  • Sulfur-smelling wells. Drillers' logs and well owners reporting rotten-egg water or pyrite in bedrock flag sulfides at depth; mapping them near the prospect chain is a free screen.
  • Satellite rust mapping. Free Sentinel-2 imagery can map iron-oxide staining in clearcuts, gravel pits and road cuts, where bare ground shows weathering sulfides.
  • Ice direction. Ice flowed roughly southwest across the belt, so gravels in the upper Chippewa valley, including around Eau Claire, carry crushed belt rock; gold grains there that are still sharp-edged point to a nearby source up-ice.
  • Old gold-bearing conglomerates. The state's list includes gold in conglomerate at Davis Hill (T44N R6W) and nuggets near Cumberland (WGNHS 1985). The old Barron Quartzite crops out in Barron County, around Cumberland (UMN thesis); ancient river conglomerates elsewhere in the world host paleoplacer gold. It is a long shot worth one sample trip.
Prospectivity model

A simple scoring model ranks eight untested spots, each more than 6 km from any recorded prospect; the top three are next to Reef (T1, T3) and Lynne (T2). The model passed a basic check: the 11 known gold-bearing sites score in the top 22% on average, against about 48% for random spots.

Method: every 1 km cell gets a weighted score from six layers: inside the volcanic belt (30% of the geophysical part), density of magnetic rock contacts (20%), closeness to northeast magnetic fault lines (25%), magnetic variety (15%), structural grain (10%), and, for the final map, closeness to the 22 copper, zinc, silver or gold prospects in the USGS database (25% of the total). The validation used only the geophysical layers, so the known sites were not scored by their own records.

T2Oneida45.64° N, 89.92° WTop 0.4%Belt, rock contactsLynne, 7 km
T3Marathon44.90° N, 89.54° WTop 0.4%Belt, NE fault trendReef, 17 km
T4Florence45.77° N, 88.14° WTop 2.1%Belt, rock contactsLaSalle Falls, 12 km
T5Taylor45.08° N, 90.27° WTop 2.5%Belt, NE fault trendBend, 35 km
T6Marathon44.80° N, 90.29° WTop 3.8%Belt, NE fault trendBend, 60 km

T8Chippewa45.25° N, 91.00° WTop 8.8%Belt, rock contactsEisenbrey, 23 km

Caveats: the belt outline was drawn around known deposits, which flatters the check somewhat, and Crandon scored only average because it has no magnetic signature. T5, T6 and T7 are the most genuinely new: none sits within 20 km of a recorded prospect. T8 is the closest to Eau Claire.

Field plan

T8 near Cornell (about 39 miles from Eau Claire) and T7 near Withee (about 45 miles) are the easiest first trips; both have river gravel or a gravel pit within a few miles. Access points are from Google Maps.

TargetFirst moves
T8, Chippewa Co.Pan Chippewa River gravel at Cornell (Mill Yard Park); look for vein-quartz boulders in fields and stone piles; check county forest rules
T7, Taylor Co.Ask the gravel pit near Withee to let you pan wash-plant fines; sample Yellow River gravel at Chequamegon Waters Flowage, 10 km north
T5, Taylor Co.Visit the Taylor County Forest office in Medford for county-land rules; pan Black River gravel at Medford
T6, Marathon Co.Look at river rocks at Cherokee County Park, 11 km northeast; ask the gravel pit near Spencer about fines; check driller logs for shallow bedrock
T3, Marathon Co.See bedrock at Rib Falls County Park; sample streams that cross the northeast fault trend southwest of Wausau
T1, Marathon Co.Same area as Target B: see the Dells gorge (look only), then sample streams east of Reef

Rules of thumb: parks and State Natural Areas are look-and-photograph only; private land and gravel pits need written permission.

Gold lore, cross-checked

Of 23 old stories and claims, the four most credible all sit near Wausau or have modern confirmation: the Eason 200-ft shaft (now the Reef prospect), the Wausau pegmatite gold, the Mosinee-area localities, and Plum Creek, where Superior Oil confirmed placer gold in 1985 but never found its bedrock source (WGNHS gold).

Credibility points: +2 inside the volcanic belt, +1 at its edge or on old northern bedrock, +2 modern confirmation, +1 a real shaft or dig on record, +1 a known glacial placer setting, +1 prospectivity model top 10%, and −2 for an unlikely host rock or a suspected hoax. Stories set in sandstone or dolomite in the south (Prairie du Chien, the McDougal farm, Knapp stock) score lowest. Locations come from old township records converted by hand and are good to about 2 km.

Best lore leads to chase:

  • The Plum Creek source. A confirmed placer with no known bedrock source is the classic setup for a discovery; ice moved roughly from the north and northeast, so the source lies up-ice.
  • The Penokee Gap camp. The Chicago Mine, Northern Belle and Brunschweiler Creek cluster in one section near Penokee Gap and were worked only briefly, 1879–81.
  • Gold tellurides around Wausau. Calaverite in a Wausau pegmatite plus tellurides at Reef hint at a wider telluride gold system.
Wild-card ideas

These are deliberately outside-the-box and untested.

The two with the most upside: the Rock Elm meteorite crater beside Plum Creek, a 6.5 km impact structure in Pierce County (USGS), as a home for Plum Creek's missing source; and ancient Cambrian beach placers in the basal Mt. Simon sandstone, which sits directly on the gold belt's eroded edge.

Idea bank

Records, ownership, methods and people worth a call, checked Oct 2026.

·

Summary

Three ideas checked out strongly: decades-old company drill data filed with the state should now be public by law, free 5-ft county LiDAR can reveal old pits under forest, and Wisconsin's 20-year dormant-mineral law can return unused severed mineral rights to surface owners. The search also turned up a new name: Badger Minerals' 2020 gold-zinc drill test at Schoepke in eastern Oneida County.

Records

The richest free record is the DNR's own project page: it shows GreenLight drilling Bend right now and a new 25-hole federal-minerals plan filed March 25, 2026, and it reveals a 2020 gold-zinc drill test at Schoepke in eastern Oneida County that most people never heard of (Wisconsin DNR).

Ownership

Wisconsin's dormant-mineral law is real and could matter: a severed mineral interest lapses to the surface owner if it goes unused for 20 years, unless the mineral owner records a statement of claim first (Wis. Stat. 706.057). This is a summary, not legal advice.

  • What counts as use: mining, recording a deal involving the interest, paying taxes on it, or recording a statement of claim.
  • How a surface owner claims it: record a claim with the county register of deeds; it takes effect when the interest lapses and is void after 6 years if no lapse occurs. The mineral owner has 3 years to contest in court.
  • Why it matters here: old 1970s–80s mining-company and railroad mineral reservations on private land in the belt may have lapsed, or may lapse. A deed search on any parcel you care about shows whether rights were severed and last used.
  • County tax-deed sales: Price and Taylor counties sell forfeited land through tax-deed sales (Price County, Taylor County). Check whether minerals were reserved before bidding; recorded mineral owners must get written notice of a tax-deed application.

Ask a Wisconsin real-estate attorney before acting on either.

Field methods

Wisconsin allows only pans and sluice boxes for recreational prospecting; motorized equipment is banned, per the Wausau prospectors' club (Clark County Press). Every method below fits that rule.

MethodHow it worksEvidenceBest place to try
Moss matsMoss on rocks in fast water traps fine gold; collect, wash out and pan. Prospectors also sell "miner's moss" mats for sluicesUsed by prospectors and in BC geological survey stream sampling (BC Geological Survey, Paydirt forum)Jump River rapids, Thornapple River below Eisenbrey
Fresh flood barsSpring high water re-sorts gravel and drops heavies at bar headsStandard placer practiceChippewa trail sites, Eau Claire to Cornell
Plowed fieldsPlowing turns up float rock; the 110 lb Vienna meteorite was found picking rocks (UW-Madison)Proven for finds, not gold specificallyFarmland over the Taylor corridor (T5–T7), with permission
Scour spotsBridge piers, culvert outlets and gravel-road ditches concentrate heaviesProspector practiceRoad crossings of belt rivers
Chippewa lobe outwashMeltwater at the ice front sorted crushed belt rock into outwashIce Age Trail guides map the Perkinstown moraine area (Ice Age Trail)Outwash south of the moraine near Perkinstown; pan gravel pits there
Gear

VLF-EM is the best-value tool for this belt: it is passive, cheap and simple, and it finds steep conductive bodies like the sulfide lenses at Flambeau and Bend (US EPA).

ToolWhat it findsStrengthsLimits
VLF-EMConductive bodies, especially steep sheets like sulfide lenses and faultsUses existing radio transmitters, no power source of its own; quick line surveysShallow, often tens of meters; fooled by fences, pipes and power lines; needs interpretation
Ground magnetometerMagnetic rock and magnetic sulfides (pyrrhotite)Rentable; pairs with the USGS magnetic grids you already haveCrandon-type ore can be non-magnetic
Soil-gas samplingGases leaking from buried sulfides through glacial coverTested at Crandon as an exploration guide (PorterGeo)Needs a lab; results vary with weather and soil

Practical order: walk VLF-EM lines across the strike of a target (northwest–southeast at Reef-trend targets), mark conductors, then check them with a magnetometer and soil samples.

People

The closest ready-made network is the Wausau Prospectors, a GPAA chapter founded in 2007 with over 100 members, one of four GPAA chapters in Wisconsin; it meets the first Saturday of each month at 11 AM (Rockhounding.org, Clark County Press).

  • Wausau Prospectors: phone (715) 340-2831 or their Facebook page. Their old website now shows spam, so skip it. The club president said almost every Wisconsin creek has fine gold, but flakes are rare.
  • GPAA: the national body runs claims and events (GPAA); a Tomah chapter and a Greenbush chapter also exist (Rockhounding.org).
  • Operators and locals: well drillers, quarry and gravel-pit operators, and county foresters. No source needed: they see bedrock, sulfides and rusty water first. Bring a printed map.
  • Companies: GreenLight is the only company actively drilling the belt, and Badger Minerals still owns land at Schoepke (Wisconsin DNR). Strong samples on ground you control could be optioned to a junior company.
